-- Per-DID Keychain account `"recovery-share-1:{did}"` (`rekey::recovery_share1_account`, the single source of this naming) stores that identity's Share 1 of the Shamir recovery split; on the client-share did:plc path this is the wallet-generated base32 **v2 share envelope** (68 chars, written with a read-back verify), while did:web ceremonies store the server-returned bare base32 (52 chars). Written by every share-writing path — the create ceremony, the did:web ceremony, the re-key flow, and the recovery epilogue (`share_recovery`) — immediately after DID promotion; per-DID so writing one identity's Share 1 can never overwrite a sibling's. Never displayed to the user

-- **Share 1 is the ONLY account the wallet writes to the iCloud-synchronizable Keychain store.** `keychain.rs` exposes two accessor families: `store_item`/`get_item`/`delete_item` (device-local) and `store_item_synced`/`get_item_synced`/`delete_item_synced` (`kSecAttrSynchronizable = true`, accessibility left at the framework default — `…ThisDeviceOnly` is mutually exclusive with syncing). These are **distinct records**, not one item with a flag: `SecItem.h` identifies an item by service + account **and** its synchronizable option, so a `store_item` value is invisible to `get_item_synced` and vice versa, and an in-place flip is undocumented/unsupported — moving a value between the stores means copying it. `keychain::syncs_to_icloud` is an enforced allowlist (`rekey::is_recovery_share1_account`): the synchronizable accessors return `SyncNotPermitted` for any other account, and `deny_list_accounts_never_sync` asserts the device key, `{did}:oauth-tokens`, `{did}:recovery-signing-key`, `ceremony-staging`, `recovery-epilogue`, and every other stored account stay off it. Share 1 is the exception because its whole job is to outlive the device that created it — one share is still one short of the 2-of-3 threshold. Reads go synced-slot-first via `rekey::load_share1`, falling back to the device-local slot; write read-backs use `rekey::read_share1_synced` and deliberately do **not** fall back, so a stale local copy can never stand in for a synchronizable write that failed. A successful synchronizable write proves only that the item carries the attribute — iOS exposes no delivery signal, so with iCloud Keychain off the item propagates nowhere, and no user-facing copy may claim it reached the Apple account

-- `lib.rs::reconcile_share1_slots` runs two best-effort, additive, idempotent launch hops in order, neither of which deletes the slot it read from: `migrate_global_share1_to_per_did` (the deprecated app-global `"recovery-share-1"` → the primary DID's per-DID slot, keyed by the legacy `"did"` item, for installs that onboarded before the per-DID unification) then `backfill_synced_share1` (each managed DID's — plus the legacy primary DID's — device-local per-DID slot → the iCloud-synchronizable slot, only when the synchronizable slot is empty **and** the local bytes decode as a valid v2 index-1 envelope via `share_recovery::decode_share1_envelope`; a bare pre-envelope did:web share cannot auto-load anyway, so syncing it would spend an iCloud secret for nothing). It runs on-device, so it reaches only a device that still holds Share 1 and opens the build at least once — an identity whose only device is already lost is never repaired and stays on Share 2 + Share 3. The recovery ceremony's auto-load (`share_recovery::auto_load_share1`) mirrors the same three slots in descending order of how far each can travel: synchronizable per-DID → device-local per-DID → deprecated app-global, each tier validated independently so a damaged higher tier cannot shadow a good lower one

-- `IdentityStore::remove_identity` deliberately does **not** delete either Share 1 slot. Removal is also reached from `forget_identity_locally`, which promises only to remove the identity from THIS device; deleting the synchronizable slot would reach every device under the Apple account and destroy a share the user may still need

-- Keychain account `"ceremony-staging"` (`share_ceremony::STAGING_ACCOUNT`) stages the in-flight ceremony's share set (JSON of the three v2 envelopes + the ceremony's handle/PDS inputs) from before the first network call until `confirm_share_backup` tears it down — the retry-idempotency anchor (same set_id across retries, no orphaned escrow) and, until teardown, the seed material's only durable home. The teardown order is load-bearing: the ceremony DID's Share 1 must be verifiably in `recovery-share-1:{did}` and the user must have confirmed Share 3 before this slot is deleted

-- Per-DID Keychain accounts `"rekey-staging:{did}"` and `"self-held-kit-staging:{did}"` (`share_ceremony`) stage the in-flight re-key's and self-held kit's share sets respectively. They are **separate slots for the same DID on purpose**: the two ceremonies disagree about who keeps Share 2 (the re-key escrows it, the kit hands it to the user), so a set staged by one must never be picked up and completed by the other. Both share `ceremony-staging`'s fail-closed contract and its load-bearing teardown order — Share 1 verifiably durable first, then the user's explicit backup confirmation, then the slot is destroyed

-- The recovery epilogue's re-escrow leg is **capability-gated**, not merely user-skippable: `share_recovery::host_offers_escrow` reads the recovered identity's current host via `pds_capabilities::probe` and records `escrow_skipped` when the host answered and advertises no `escrow`. The asymmetry is deliberate — a host that could NOT be asked (`reached: false`) is still attempted, because treating a transient outage as "no escrow" would silently downgrade a Custos account's recovery posture, whereas attempting a deposit against a PDS with no such route fails a leg that was never going to succeed and blocks the Share 1 write behind it

-- Keychain account `"recovery-epilogue"` (`share_recovery::EPILOGUE_ACCOUNT`) is the durable record of an in-flight recovery rotation epilogue (JSON: DID, old/new recovery key ids, the three NEW v2 envelopes, per-step completion flags). Written by `recover_identity` before it returns and deleted only by `confirm_recovery_backup` after the NEW Share 1 is verified durable in the recovered DID's per-DID `recovery-share-1:{did}` slot, so an app kill anywhere in the epilogue resumes on next launch (`get_pending_recovery_epilogue` + the `recover_epilogue` step). Fail-closed like `ceremony-staging`: a present-but-unreadable record errors (`EPILOGUE_CORRUPT`) and is preserved — it may hold the only copy of a share set the swap op already bound to the DID

SOURCE_AUTH_FAILED is a rejected password `createSession` on the source PDS (wrong password / app-password used); TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED means the source account has email 2FA — the PDS emailed a code and the UI prompts for it, re-invoking `authenticate_source_pds` with the `auth_factor_token`; ACCOUNT_MISMATCH means the entered credentials signed in to a different account than the one being claimed (`createSession`'s returned DID ≠ the claim DID — refused before any PLC op); INSECURE_SOURCE_URL means the source PDS endpoint (from the DID doc) isn't HTTPS, so the password is refused rather than sent in cleartext (loopback excepted); INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE is a PLC-op endpoint refusing the token for scope reasons, surfaced distinctly rather than masquerading as "failed to send verification email"; RATE_LIMITED (carries `retryAfter`) and SERVER_ERROR (carries the server's own `message`) are the status-classified surfaces — a 429/other non-2xx from a PLC-op or source login now names the real reason instead of the connectivity boilerplate. An empty set deletes the entry; a corrupt/unreadable entry reads as empty (the marker is a best-effort safety net, never a launch blocker)

-- The five **notification** Keychain accounts are app-global, not per-DID (`notifications::NOTIFICATION_ACCOUNTS` is the inventory, and `keychain.rs`'s `notification_material_never_syncs` reads that constant rather than a copy of it): `notification-device-uuid` (the stable identifier the server keys registrations on — it must outlive every identity that uses it, which is why it is not the transient `devices.id`), `notification-key-priv` (the raw P-256 scalar), `notification-sender-keys` (the versioned per-host pin document), `notification-apns-token` (lowercase hex), and `notification-failures` (the Notification Service Extension's bounded breadcrumb log — **the one slot the extension writes and the app only reads**, hence the same locked-screen protection class: a failure is recorded in the moment it happens, which is on a locked screen). The private key, the pin document, and the extension's failure log are written under **`kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`** via `keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock` — everything the extension touches, since it runs on a locked screen; the device uuid and the APNs token use ordinary `store_item`. **None of them ever syncs** — the private key most pointedly, since it is readable on a locked screen and syncing it would place a passcode-free key in the Apple account for no recovery benefit (a replacement device mints its own on first registration). The pin document is read **fail-open** (corrupt ⇒ empty), the deliberate inverse of `ceremony-staging`: it holds public keys the server re-serves on the next contact, so refusing to read it would forfeit the very re-pin that repairs it

-- `keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock` is **not a third store**. It writes into the same device-local store as `store_item` and is read by the same `get_item`/`delete_item`; only the item's protection class differs, and one account written through both accessors is one record whose class is the last write's. The write is delete-then-add rather than the crate's add-or-update, because `SecItemUpdate` cannot change an existing item's protection class — an update would silently keep whatever class the first write set, which is the one thing this accessor exists to control. `keychain::Accessibility` + `accessibility_of` are test-only, since iOS never reports a class back and the in-memory double is the only place the locked-screen readability is assertable

Neither notification command is biometric-gated — nothing is signed and no identity material is exposed, and a prompt on the onboarding-completion path would be a demand the user cannot connect to anything they did

The cadence is a **security property**, not housekeeping: registration re-pins on the same contact, and until a device re-pins, a compromised sender key plus a colluding relay can forge notification content for it

Neither app has an installed base below 17; a per-target split (extension at 17, app lower, runtime-gated registration) buys nothing but complexity

-- `migrate::guard_migration_op` enforces a STRICT allowlist before signing: (1) `rotationKeys[0]` == device key, (2) device key is in the DID's current rotationKeys (else `WalletNotAuthorized` → orchestrator falls back to the interop path), (3) every other proposed rotation key was recommended by the destination, (4) alsoKnownAs preserved, (5) only the `atproto_pds` service is touched. This is the inverse of `claim.rs`'s guard, which forbids the very key/service changes a migration requires

So **alsoKnownAs may change; rotationKeys, verificationMethods, and services must not** — the exact opposite of migration's invariant 4 (which requires alsoKnownAs preserved). The build assembles the op with every non-alsoKnownAs field passed through as current==proposed, so the guard proves the op is a pure handle change

## Troubleshooting
### `cargo tauri ios dev` fails with "Connection refused"

-You launched the Xcode build manually (clicking Run in Xcode) instead of through `cargo tauri ios dev`. Xcode's "Build Rust Code" phase calls `cargo tauri ios xcode-script`, which connects back to the `cargo tauri ios dev` process via JSON-RPC. There is no server to connect to if the build was not initiated by `cargo tauri ios dev`.
+You clicked Run in Xcode. The "Build Rust Code" phase connects back to the
+`cargo tauri ios dev` process via JSON-RPC; there is no server unless that process started
+the build. Always launch from the terminal.
-**Fix:** Always use `cargo tauri ios dev` from the terminal. Do not click Run in Xcode.
+### `error: can't find crate for 'core'` — `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` missing
+Resolved by the rustup migration (see First-Time Setup). If it appears on a fresh clone,
+you entered the dev shell from a subdirectory — re-enter from the workspace root so
+`CARGO_HOME` resolves.
-### `error: can't find crate for 'core'` — `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` target not installed
+### `simctl` not found / `xcrun simctl list` fails
-The Nix `rust-default` package (used by `languages.rust` in devenv) does not ship iOS cross-compilation stdlibs. This was the historical state of the project before the rustup migration.
+The Nix Darwin stdenv points `DEVELOPER_DIR`/`SDKROOT` at a tool-less apple-sdk stub, and
+`xcode-select -p`/`xcrun` honor those env vars above the system Xcode selection.
+`ios-env.sh` (sourced by `enterShell`) strips them when they point into `/nix/store`. If it
+persists: `echo $DEVELOPER_DIR` — a Nix store path means re-enter the shell from the root.

-**Fix:** Already resolved. `devenv.nix` uses `pkgs.rustup` with project-local `RUSTUP_HOME`/`CARGO_HOME`. On first `nix develop`, `enterShell` runs `rustup toolchain install` which reads `rust-toolchain.toml` and installs `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` stdlib automatically.
-If you see this after a fresh clone: make sure you entered the dev shell from the **workspace root** (not from `apps/identity-wallet/`) so that `CARGO_HOME` resolves correctly.
-### `error: tool 'simctl' not found` or `xcrun simctl list` fails

-The Nix devenv's Darwin setup hooks override `DEVELOPER_DIR` (and `SDKROOT`) to a Nix apple-sdk stub that has no runtime tools. The `xcbuild` xcrun shim in PATH delegates to `$DEVELOPER_DIR/usr/bin/xcrun` — if `DEVELOPER_DIR` points at a Nix stub, it fails.

-**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `devenv.nix`'s `enterShell` sources `apps/identity-wallet/scripts/ios-env.sh`. The catch: `/usr/bin/xcode-select -p` and `/usr/bin/xcrun` both **honor `DEVELOPER_DIR` above the system Xcode selection**, so calling them by absolute path is not enough — they echo the Nix stub straight back. `ios-env.sh` first **unsets `DEVELOPER_DIR` when it points into `/nix/store`**, so `xcode-select -p` falls through to the real Xcode selection; it then re-exports `DEVELOPER_DIR` to that real path. (A genuine Xcode-provided `DEVELOPER_DIR` — not under `/nix/store` — is left untouched, so the Xcode Run Script keeps Xcode's own value.)
-If you still see this: verify with `echo $DEVELOPER_DIR` inside the dev shell. If it shows a Nix store path, exit and re-enter the shell from the workspace root.
### `sandbox-exec: sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted` (Tauri ios-api build)

-Swift Package Manager sandboxes its manifest compilation using `sandbox-exec`. On macOS 26 (Tahoe), `sandbox_apply()` returns `EPERM` in this context, causing `swift-rs`'s build script (used by Tauri) to fail with "Failed to compile swift package Tauri".
+macOS 26 returns `EPERM` for SPM's manifest-compile sandbox. Fixed by the local `swift-rs`
+patch (`apps/identity-wallet/swift-rs-patch/`, wired via `[patch.crates-io]`) adding
+`--disable-sandbox`; see `docs/ios-upstream-bugs.md`. Remove when upstream ships a fix.

-**Fix:** Already resolved and applied automatically. A local patch of `swift-rs` 1.0.7 at `apps/identity-wallet/swift-rs-patch/` adds `--disable-sandbox` to the `swift build` invocation inside `SwiftLinker::link`. The workspace `Cargo.toml` wires this in via `[patch.crates-io]`. See `docs/ios-upstream-bugs.md` for details. Remove the patch entry when swift-rs ships a fix upstream.
+### `Failed to update the excludes stack …` (Xcode user script sandbox)
+Xcode 14+'s `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING=YES` blocks Cargo's `readdir()` on macOS 26. The
+template sets it to `NO`; `just ios-check` verifies.
-### `Failed to update the excludes stack to see if a path is excluded` (Xcode user script sandbox)
+### `Undefined symbols ... _SC*` / `_ASWebAuthenticationSession*` at `Ld`

-Xcode 14+ enables `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING=YES` by default in generated projects, wrapping Run Script build phases in `sandbox-exec`. On macOS 26 (Tahoe), this sandbox blocks Cargo's `readdir()` calls during package fingerprinting, producing:
+An Apple framework a Rust crate needs isn't linked in the Xcode project. Host builds link
+fine (rustc honors the crate's `#[link]`); on iOS, Xcode does the final link of the
+staticlib and never sees that directive. Fix by adding the framework to
+`bundle > iOS > frameworks` in `tauri.conf.json` (the template renders `OTHER_LDFLAGS` and
+xcodegen link deps from it) and re-running init + postinit — never hand-edit
+`OTHER_LDFLAGS` (a second assignment shadows the first; `just ios-check` detects it).
-error: failed to determine package fingerprint for build script for identity-wallet v0.1.0
-Caused by: Failed to update the excludes stack to see if a path is excluded

-**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template sets `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING: NO`, which every `cargo tauri ios init` renders into the generated project; `just ios-check` verifies the setting is in place.
-### `Undefined symbols ... _SC*` / `_ASWebAuthenticationSession*` — an Apple framework not linked at `Ld`

-The Rust code compiles, then Xcode's link step fails with `Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:` naming Apple framework symbols — e.g. `_SCDynamicStore...` / `_SCNetworkReachability...` (Apple's `SystemConfiguration.framework`, which the `system-configuration` crate needs — pulled in transitively by `hickory-resolver` for system DNS config and `reqwest` for system proxy detection), or `_ASWebAuthenticationSessionErrorDomain` (Apple's `AuthenticationServices.framework`, which the vendored `tauri-plugin-auth-session` needs via `objc2-authentication-services` / `ASWebAuthenticationSession`).

-Host builds (`cargo test` / `cargo build`) link fine because **rustc** does the final link and honors the crate's `#[link(name = "...", kind = "framework")]`. On iOS the crate is built as a `staticlib` (`libapp.a`) and **Xcode** does the final link — it never sees that embedded directive, so the framework must be declared in the Xcode project or the symbols stay undefined. A `build.rs` `cargo:rustc-link-lib=framework=...` does NOT help (same staticlib → Xcode gap).

-**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template renders `OTHER_LDFLAGS = "$(inherited) -framework SystemConfiguration -framework AuthenticationServices"` from `bundle > iOS > frameworks` in `tauri.conf.json` (the same list also produces xcodegen `sdk:` link dependencies), and `just ios-check` verifies every listed framework. The historical footgun this design removes: `bundle.iOS.frameworks` used to seed only a FRESH project.yml, because `cargo tauri ios init` preserves an existing one — with the custom template, project.yml is re-rendered from config on every init, so the config is now the enforced mechanism. To link another Apple framework a new Rust dep requires, **add it to `bundle > iOS > frameworks` in `tauri.conf.json`** and re-run `cargo tauri ios init` + `just ios-postinit` — never hand-edit `OTHER_LDFLAGS` in the generated project (a second `OTHER_LDFLAGS` assignment for the same build config shadows, not appends to, the first, silently dropping a framework — `just ios-check` detects that state).
### `libapp.a ... is not permitted` / `Invalid bundle structure` on TestFlight upload

-`cargo tauri ios build` succeeds and `xcrun altool` then rejects the upload (HTTP 409): *"The 'Obsign.app/libapp.a' binary file is not permitted. Your app cannot contain standalone executables or libraries."* (tauri#13578.)
+cargo-mobile2 lists `Externals` with no `buildPhase`, so XcodeGen infers `resources` and
+copies the raw staticlib into the bundle, which App Store validation forbids (tauri#13578).
+The template sets `Externals → buildPhase: none`; the `framework: libapp.a` link dependency
+is kept. `just ios-check` verifies both layers.

-cargo-mobile2 lists the `Externals` directory (which holds the Rust staticlib `libapp.a`) as a project source with **no explicit `buildPhase`**, so XcodeGen infers `resources` and copies the raw `.a` into the `.app` — which App Store validation forbids. The library is also (correctly) **linked** via the separate `framework: libapp.a` entry + `LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATHS`, so excluding it from resources is safe.
+### `base64: invalid option -- 'o'` during signing

-**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template sets `Externals → buildPhase: none`, so xcodegen never emits a `libapp.a in Resources` entry (the `framework: libapp.a` link dependency is kept). `just ios-check` verifies both layers.
-### `base64: invalid option -- 'o'` during `cargo tauri ios build` signing

-The build reads `IOS_CERTIFICATE` and fails decoding it: `base64: invalid option -- 'o'`. In the Nix dev shell, GNU coreutils `base64` shadows macOS's BSD `base64` in `PATH`, but Tauri's cert decode uses BSD-only flags (`-i`/`-o`). (CI is unaffected — the runner has no Nix.)

-**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `scripts/ios-env.sh` (under `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD=1`) shims `/usr/bin/base64` ahead of the Nix one via a tiny symlink dir on `PATH` — surgical (only `base64`), leaving every other Nix tool untouched.
+GNU coreutils `base64` shadows BSD `base64` in the Nix shell, and Tauri's cert decode uses
+BSD-only flags. `ios-env.sh` (under `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD=1`) shims `/usr/bin/base64` ahead of
+the Nix one.

Second of the two MM-495 per-file PRs (part 1: #498). `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md` drops from **26,984 to 3,818 words (−86%)** — past the issue's 60–70% estimate because this file described each module up to *three* times (the Exposes bullets, the Key Files list, and the Invariants section all restated the same ~35 modules). Eliminating the triple-statement is where the extra reduction comes from; the constraint that matters — zero information loss — was verified fact-by-fact before each entry shrank.

## What moved where

- **src-tauri modules**: every module now carries a `//!` doc holding its former AGENTS.md facts (the existing `//` headers were merged in, not duplicated). `keychain.rs`'s doc is now the **canonical Keychain account inventory** (app-global accounts, the per-DID `"{did}:suffix"` pattern, the synced-store allowlist, protection classes). Each of the **seven strict pre-sign guards** carries its full allowlist in its own module, with the mirror/inverse relationships preserved.
- **Frontend**: the home-surface screens, `+page.svelte` (a step-graph comment now heads the file), the `src/lib` utilities, and the harness (per-scenario purpose notes now live on the scenario definitions in `scenarios.ts`). Much of the frontend was already documented in place — those entries were pure dedup.
- **AGENTS.md keeps**: the map, the harness runbook, workstation setup/workflow/CI (trimmed), the cross-cutting invariants (bundle identity, access-group ordering, frozen iCloud container, the one wire-contract rule replacing ~25 serde-sentence repetitions), and the symptom-keyed Troubleshooting section.

## Drift found and fixed along the way

Corrected in the module docs to match the code:
- the blob-backup manifest checkpoints every 25 blobs, not "after every blob";
- MyAgentsScreen's locked-load unlock calls `sovereignLogin` directly, not `unlockIdentity`;
- `check_identity_status` lives in `plc_monitor` (lib.rs only registers it);
- `remove_identity` clears ten per-DID entries now (the `self-held-kit` marker postdated the "nine");
- `MigrationError`'s inline variant list omitted `BLOB_DRAIN_INCOMPLETE`/`BACKUP_UNAVAILABLE`;
- the harness proxy header over-claimed the proxied subset.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p identity-wallet` under the iOS host env ✓ (comment-only Rust diff)
- `pnpm check` — 463 files, 0 errors ✓
- `pnpm test` — 259 passed, incl. the harness fake-coverage gate ✓
- `rustfmt --check` on all 37 touched `.rs` files ✓
- `just ticket-ref-check` ✓; changelog gate ✓ (`changelog.d/mm-495-wallet.changed.md` — wallet src is a shipped surface even for comment-only changes)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"

## Prose / Docs

content.text:
MM-495 is done — both halves shipped as their own PRs, and the issue is In Review with both attached.

## What landed

**[PR #498](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/498) — `crates/pds/AGENTS.md`: 16,624 → 5,260 words (−68%).** The survey inverted the issue's "pure dedup" expectation: outside the documented minority (firehose, blob_*, capabilities…), most files in the identity/auth/db/routes tables had **no** module doc at all, so the bulk of the diff is ~100 `//!` docs created or converted from plain `//` headers. Pure-dedup wins: the firehose essay (already homed in `firehose/mod.rs`'s item docs, plus a new emission-map paragraph) and the metrics table (a self-declared mirror of `metrics::names`, now collapsed — that "change them together" drift hazard is gone).

**[PR #499](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/499) — `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md`: 26,984 → 3,818 words (−86%).** Past the 60–70% estimate because this file described each module up to *three* times (Exposes + Key Files + Invariants); the triple-statement collapsed into one module map, and ~25 repetitions of the serde-contract sentence became one stated rule. `keychain.rs` is now the canonical Keychain account inventory, and each of the seven strict pre-sign guards carries its full allowlist in its own module.

**Zero information loss, and a bonus:** verifying facts against code before moving them surfaced ~10 stale AGENTS.md claims (read-after-write lag-header condition, blob-backup checkpoint cadence, a mis-attributed command, incomplete error-variant lists, stale function homes) — all corrected in the module docs to match the source.

**Verification:** both branches pass `cargo test --workspace` / `cargo check` (wallet under the iOS host env), `clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, rustfmt on every touched file, `pnpm check` + all 259 frontend tests, docs-check, ticket-ref-check, and the changelog gate (fragments added — `crates/*/src` and wallet source are gated paths even for comment-only diffs).

## One thing you should know

A local **PostToolUse "secrets hygiene" hook misfired three times** during the run, keying on filenames (`jwt_secret.rs`, `admin_revoke_credentials.rs`, `get_recommended_did_credentials.rs`) and instructing agents to gitignore and `chmod 600` those tracked source files. All three agents refused — the files contain no secrets, and complying would have removed route handlers from version control. Worth checking that hook's matching rules; I've noted it in project memory.

That closes out MM-494 and MM-495 from this session (PRs #497, #498, #499 awaiting your review). MM-496 (marketing-site audit) is the remaining follow-up from the prose corrective.

The CodeRabbit round on [PR #499](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/499) is fully dispositioned — 13 of 14 accepted and fixed in commit `b48626ca`, one declined with a reply. PR #498 has no unresolved threads.

**What the accepted fixes were.** All doc-wording corrections, and genuinely good catches — CodeRabbit was auditing the freshly-moved module docs against the code, and several of its hits were drift inherited from the *old* AGENTS.md text we'd transposed faithfully:

- The ceremony share set is staged before `POST /v1/dids`, not "before any network call" (the read-only signing-key GET precedes staging) — fixed in `lib.rs`, the inline comment, and `share_ceremony.rs`.
- `remove_identity` writes the `forgotten-dids` tombstone *before* touching the index (the doc said index-first), and only per-DID `IdentityStore` methods require registration.
- `OAuthClient::new_bearer` still initializes the shared DPoP keypair, so the "DPoP constructor never called in production" claim is now scoped to the DPoP mode itself.
- The "password used for exactly one request" claim didn't survive the email-2FA retry, which re-sends it with `authFactorToken` — fixed in both `source_login.rs` and `password_unlock.rs`.
- `repo_backup`'s CAR check verifies `sig` *presence*, not the signature — the doc now says structural validation, with the destination import as the authenticating consumer.
- The three signing sites without one of the seven named guards (tombstone, recovery override, share-recovery rotations) now state their *actual* pre-sign constraints — self-verification, and op construction that copies everything but rotationKeys from authoritative state — rather than being left looking unguarded. I didn't invent guards that don't exist.
- Smaller ones: disaster recovery's `describeServer` is asked of the destination PDS (not "plc.directory alone"), the unreached-probe rule is scoped to the capability probe, `+page.svelte`'s flow map now shows did:web skipping `shamir_backup`, `share_ceremony`'s Share 2 escrow claim is scoped to the escrowing ceremonies, and the changelog fragment says "Obsign".

**The one decline: CocoaPods.** It wanted `sudo gem install cocoapods` replaced with "use the `pod` from the Nix/devenv shell" — but devenv doesn't provide `pod`, the instruction predates this PR, and the iOS toolchain is deliberately de-Nixed, so the suggested wording would document a binary that doesn't exist. I replied on the thread with that reasoning and offered to file a follow-up if you want CocoaPods added to devenv.

Verification after the fixes: wallet `cargo check` and `svelte-check` (463 files, 0 errors) both green. Heads-up per the batch-triage playbook: the fix push will trigger a fresh CodeRabbit pass, which tends to find one more micro-nit.

1. **`identity_removal.rs`** — I'd lumped the wipe-last ordering in as a "pre-sign check". The doc now states them as two things.

2. **`share_ceremony.rs`** — my staging-boundary sentence generalized the create ceremony's `POST /v1/dids` to all three ceremonies, but each has its own state-creating boundary: create's `POST /v1/dids`, the re-key's rotation-op submit followed by the escrow `PUT`, and the kit's rotation-op submit (no `/v1/*` call — I pointed at `self_held_kit.rs` for its network posture rather than repeating it, which also avoids baiting a round 3 on the describeServer probe).

I fear that the user-facing prose may come off too much as generated, and perhaps might not actually be targeting the correct audience. and then within the codebase, we often have dense comment blocks with a bunch of context that is vaguely useful-shaped but often just a lot to read. # Writing for a Technical Audience

## Overview

**Core principle:** Technical writing must be clear, concise, and authentic. Clarity and technical depth are not opposites - you can have both. Avoid AI writing patterns that make content feel robotic or inauthentic.
￼
**Why this matters:** Developers value their time. Clear documentation builds trust. AI-like writing patterns (identified through research) make content feel generic and untrustworthy. Technical depth without clarity frustrates users. Clarity without depth leaves them stuck.

## When to Use

**Use this skill when:**
- Writing API documentation or references
- Creating guides, tutorials, or how-to content
- Documenting code, features, or architecture
- Writing technical blog posts or articles
- Reviewing technical content for clarity

**Trigger symptoms:**
- "Does this sound too robotic?"
- Writing feels formal or stiff
- Using phrases like "delve into" or "leverage"
- Explaining obvious things instead of getting to the point
- Uncertain if content is clear enough

## The Three Pillars

### 1. Clarity

Developers should understand on first read. No re-reading required.

**Techniques:**
- Short sentences (15-20 words average)
- Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences)
- Active voice over passive
- One concept per paragraph
- Define technical terms on first use

### 2. Conciseness

Every word serves a purpose. Remove noise and filler.

**Techniques:**
- Delete throat-clearing ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- Cut hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- Remove marketing fluff ("powerful," "robust," "seamless")
- Use direct language ("use" not "leverage," "show" not "illuminate")

### 3. Consistency

Same terminology, structure, and voice throughout.

**Techniques:**
- Pick one term and stick to it (not "endpoint," "URL," "route" interchangeably)
- Use consistent code formatting
- Maintain same tone across all content
- Follow established patterns for similar content types

## Avoid AI Writing Patterns

Research shows specific phrases and structures that readers identify as AI-generated. Avoid these to maintain authenticity.

### AI Phrases to Never Use

| AI Phrase | Why It's Bad | Use Instead |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| "delve into" | Overly formal, 269x spike post-ChatGPT | "explore," "examine," "look at" |
| "leverage" | Corporate jargon | "use," "take advantage of" |
| "robust" / "seamless" | Vague marketing adjectives | Be specific about what you mean |
| "at its core" | Condescending simplification | "fundamentally" (use rarely) or delete |
| "cutting-edge" / "revolutionary" | Empty hype | Describe actual features |
| "streamline" / "optimize" | Vague promises | "speed up," "reduce," "improve" |
| "foster" / "cultivate" | Bland corporate speak | Use direct action verbs |
| "unlock the potential" | Cliched metaphor | State specific outcome |
| "in today's fast-paced world" | Generic filler | Delete entirely |
| "needless to say" | If needless, don't say it | Delete |

### Throat-Clearing to Delete

**Never start with:**
- "Let me explain..."
- "It's important to note that..."
- "It's worth noting..."
- "In essence..."
- "Let's explore..."

**Fix:** Start with substance. Delete the preamble.

### Hedging Language to Eliminate

| Hedged | Confident |
|--------|-----------|
| "I think we should..." | "We should..." |
| "It would be great if..." | "Please do X" |
| "Should be able to..." | "Can complete..." |
| "Basically..." | Delete it |
| "Generally speaking..." | Be specific or remove |
| "One might argue..." | "This indicates..." |

**Why hedging fails:** Makes you sound uncertain even when you're correct. State facts directly.

### Transition Word Overuse

AI defaults to formal Victorian-era connectors. Use simpler alternatives or break paragraphs.

| Overused AI | Better |
|------------|--------|
| Moreover / Furthermore | Plus, also, and |
| However / Nevertheless | But, though, still |
| Additionally | And, plus |
| Consequently / As a result | So, then |
| That being said | But (or delete) |
| Indeed / Interestingly | Often delete entirely |
| In conclusion | End cleanly without announcing it |

## Technical Writing Patterns

### Explain WHY for These Cases

**ALWAYS explain why when:**

1. **Design decisions with tradeoffs**
   - Good: "We use pagination instead of cursors because it's simpler for most use cases and maintains consistent ordering"
   - Bad: "We use pagination" (no context for when to deviate)

2. **Non-obvious patterns**
   - Good: "Row Level Security must be enabled on all tables exposed via the Data API because it enforces security at the database level, preventing bypass through direct SQL access"
   - Bad: "Enable RLS on all tables" (why?)

3. **Breaking from conventions**
   - Good: "This API uses POST for reads because GET requests can't include request bodies in some HTTP clients"
   - Bad: "Use POST to fetch data" (violates REST conventions without justification)

**When "how" alone suffices:**
- Mechanical steps with no alternatives ("Click Save")
- Standard practices ("Use npm install")
- When you genuinely don't know why (document behavior, note uncertainty)

### Code Examples: One Excellent Example

**Don't:**
- Implement in 5 languages
- Create fill-in-the-blank templates
- Write perfect-world examples with no error handling

**Do:**
- One complete, runnable example
- Include error handling
- Show realistic usage
- Comment WHY, not what

**Good Example Pattern:**

```python
# Good: Complete, realistic, explains why
try:
    response = await fetch_user(user_id)
    # Check status before assuming success - API returns 200 for "not found"
    if response.status != 200:
        raise APIError(f"Failed to fetch user: {response.status}")
    return response.json()
except NetworkError as e:
    # Network failures are retryable - log and re-raise for retry logic
    logger.warning(f"Network error fetching user {user_id}: {e}")
    raise
```

**Bad Example Pattern:**

```python
# Bad: Perfect world, no context, brittle
response = await fetch_user(user_id)
return response.json()
```

### Progressive Disclosure

Layer complexity. Simple first, then depth.

**Pattern:**
1. **Basic explanation** - what it does, core concept
2. **Simple example** - minimal working code
3. **Advanced section** - edge cases, configuration, tradeoffs
4. **Reference** - complete API surface

**Good:**
```markdown
## Authentication

All API requests require an API key in the Authorization header:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer REDACTED" https://api.example.com/users
```

### Advanced: Token Rotation

For production systems, rotate API keys every 90 days...
```

**Bad:**
```markdown
## Authentication

Authentication can be performed using several methods including API keys, OAuth 2.0, or JWT tokens. The choice depends on your security requirements, user experience goals, and architectural constraints. Let's explore each option...
```

(Too much upfront. Start simple.)

## Anti-Patterns from Real Documentation

### 1. Assumes Too Much

**Bad:**
> "Simply connect your ETLOrchestrator to the HydraNode endpoint. Once a connection is established, instantiate a DataStream by passing your KinesisConfiguration."

**Why it fails:** Jargon firehose with no definitions, no links, no onramp for beginners.

**Fix:** Define terms, link to prerequisites, provide Getting Started guide.

### 2. Perfect World Examples

**Bad:**
```javascript
const myFile = document.getElementById('file-input').files[0];
const response = await uploadFile('/api/upload', myFile);
console.log('File uploaded successfully!');
```

**Why it fails:** No error handling, ignores edge cases (no file selected, network failure, file too large).

**Fix:** Wrap in try-catch, check response status, handle undefined files.

### 3. Vague and Unhelpful

**Bad:**
- `getUser(userId)`: "Gets a user by their ID."
- `class DataProcessor`: "A class for processing data."
- `processData(data)`: "Processes the data."

**Why it fails:** Tautological. Says nothing beyond the function name.

**Fix:** Describe behavior, parameters, return values, exceptions. "Fetches user record from database, returns null if user doesn't exist. Throws AuthError if API key lacks read permissions."

## Pro-Examples from Industry Leaders

### Supabase (Clarity + Depth)

> "Row Level Security (RLS) is a PostgreSQL feature that allows you to control which rows a user can access in a table. When you enable RLS on a table, all SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations are subject to a security policy. A policy is a SQL expression that returns a boolean value. If the expression returns true, the operation is allowed to proceed. If it returns false or null, the operation is denied."

**Why it works:** Defines RLS, explains scope (CRUD operations), defines mechanism (policy = SQL boolean expression). Dense with information, perfectly clear.

### Stripe (Predictable Contract)

> "Stripe uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. In general: Codes in the 2xx range indicate success. Codes in the 4xx range indicate an error that failed given the information provided. Codes in the 5xx range indicate an error with Stripe's servers."

**Why it works:** Establishes predictable contract for fundamental API behavior. Technical, precise, immediately useful.

### Astro (Anticipates Questions)

> "You can run create-astro anywhere on your machine, so you don't have to create an empty directory for your project first. If you don't have an empty directory yet, the wizard will help you create one."

**Why it works:** Anticipates common beginner question ("Do I need to make a folder first?") and answers it proactively.

### Tailwind CSS (Teaches Philosophy)

> "The biggest maintainability concern when using a utility-first approach is managing commonly repeated utility combinations. The traditional approach is to extract repeated utilities into a component class. We believe that @apply should be used sparingly. The best way to manage repeated utility combinations is to create reusable components with a templating language."

**Why it works:** Identifies problem, presents common solution, explains why that solution is suboptimal, guides toward better approach. Teaches philosophy, not just features.

## Writing That Feels Human

### Use Contractions

**AI defaults to:**
- "It is important that you do not..."
- "You will need to..."

**Human writing:**
- "It's important that you don't..."
- "You'll need to..."

### Vary Sentence Length

**AI writes:**
Every paragraph is 3-4 sentences. Every sentence is 15-20 words. Everything feels perfectly balanced and rhythmic in an uncanny way.

**Human writes:**
Short sentences create emphasis. Longer sentences provide context, explanation, or explore nuance that requires more breathing room. Mix them. Create rhythm naturally.

### Add Personality

**AI avoids:**
- First person ("I," "we")
- Opinions
- Personal anecdotes
- Humor

**Human includes:**
- "We tried the obvious solution first and it failed"
- "I found this approach more practical because..."
- Opinions grounded in experience
- Self-aware observations

### Break Grammar Rules Intentionally

**AI never:**
- Starts sentences with "And" or "But"
- Uses sentence fragments
- Ends with prepositions

**Human does:**
- "And that's exactly the point." (emphasis)
- "This is what we're dealing with." (natural)

### Be Specific

**AI writes vaguely:**
- "This approach offers significant benefits"
- "Companies have seen improved results"

**Human writes specifically:**
- "We reduced latency from 450ms to 120ms"
- "Three team members raised concerns about X"

## Code Comments and Documentation

### Punctuation

Always use periods at the end of code comments.

```typescript
// Good: Validates user input before processing.
// Bad: validates user input before processing
```

### Headings

Use sentence case in all headings. Never title case.

```markdown
Good: ## Error handling patterns
Bad:  ## Error Handling Patterns

Good: ### When to use async
Bad:  ### When To Use Async
```

### Error Messages

Format error messages as lowercase sentence fragments. They compose naturally when chained.

```
Good: failed to parse configuration: invalid JSON at line 42
Bad:  Failed to Parse Configuration: Invalid JSON at Line 42
```

The lowercase format works because errors often chain: `"operation failed: " + innerError.message` reads correctly.

## Red Flags - Review Checklist

Before publishing, check for these issues:

- [ ] No AI phrases ("delve," "leverage," "robust," "at its core")
- [ ] No throat-clearing openings ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- [ ] No hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- [ ] No marketing fluff ("powerful," "revolutionary," "cutting-edge")
- [ ] Sentence length varies (not all 15-20 words)
- [ ] Paragraph length varies (not all 3-4 sentences)
- [ ] Contractions used naturally ("it's" not "it is")
- [ ] Active voice, clear actors (not "it can be seen that")
- [ ] Code examples include error handling
- [ ] WHY explained for design decisions
- [ ] Technical terms defined on first use
- [ ] Specific numbers/names/details (not vague claims)
- [ ] Read aloud test - does it sound natural?
- [ ] Code comments end with periods
- [ ] Headings use sentence case (not Title Case)
- [ ] Error messages are lowercase sentence fragments

## Common Mistakes and Fixes

| Mistake | Reality | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| "Just being thorough with explanations" | You're explaining obvious things. | Delete explanations of what developers already know. |
| "Keeping it professional with formal language" | Formal = robotic. | Use contractions, conversational tone, natural language. |
| "Covering all the edge cases upfront" | Overwhelms reader. | Basic case first, advanced section for edge cases. |
| "Using precise technical terminology" | Jargon without definitions loses readers. | Define terms on first use, link to glossary. |
| "Being careful with hedging language" | Hedging makes you sound uncertain. | State facts directly. Remove qualifiers. |
| "Perfect code examples look cleaner" | Perfect world examples are brittle in practice. | Include error handling, show realistic usage. |
| "More examples = more helpful" | Too many examples = noise. | One excellent, complete example beats five shallow ones. |

## Summary

**Technical writing in three rules:**

1. **Clear and concise** - Short sentences, short paragraphs, active voice, no filler
2. **Authentic voice** - Contractions, varied rhythm, personality, specific details
3. **Explain why** - Design decisions, tradeoffs, non-obvious patterns need justification

**Avoid AI markers:** No "delve," "leverage," "robust." No throat-clearing. No hedging. No formal transitions.

**One excellent example** beats five mediocre ones. Include error handling. Show realistic usage.

**Technical depth + clarity are not opposites.** You can have both. Supabase, Stripe, and Cloudflare prove this daily.

**Read aloud test:** If it sounds robotic or overly formal, rewrite it.

content.content: 1 --- 2 title: Getting started 3 description: Create a new identity or bring an existing one into Obsign. 4 --- 5 6 When you open Obsign, it asks one question — **what's your situation?** — and 7 routes you from your answer, rather than making you name the ceremony you need: 8 9 13 14 - **Starting fresh** — make a brand-new identity from scratch, on a server you 15 choose. 16 - **I have an account somewhere** — take custody of an account you already have, 17 wherever it is hosted. Your device becomes its master key; the account stays on 18 its current server. 19 - **I lost access to my wallet** — bring an identity back onto a new device using 20 any two of its three backup shares (see 21 [Recovering with two shares](/user/backup/#recovering-with-two-shares)). 22 - **My server is gone** — your host has disappeared and you need the identity 23 somewhere else. 24 25 Taking custody of an existing account is not the same as moving it. It changes 26 *who holds the keys*; moving changes *where the account lives*, and you do that 27 later from the identity's own screen (see 28 [Migrating your identity](/user/migration/)). 29 30 If you already have identities in the wallet, tap **Add an identity** at the 31 bottom of your identity list to reach this screen again. 32 33 37 38 ## Create an identity 39 40 1. Open Obsign and choose **Starting fresh**. 41 2. Follow the prompts to pick a handle on an available domain and set up your 42 account. 43 3. Obsign generates your identity key **on your device** and seals it. The key 44 never leaves your device unencrypted. 45 4. As part of setup, Obsign walks you through **backing up your recovery key** and 46 won't let you finish until you've saved your share — see 47 [2-of-3 Shamir backup](/user/backup/). 48 49 :::tip 50 Backup isn't a separate step you do later — it's built into adding your identity, 51 which is exactly the right time. Save your share somewhere durable when Obsign 52 prompts you, not after you've lost a device. 53 ::: 54 55 :::note 56 Creating an identity needs a **Custos** server. Your device has to author the 57 identity's very first record and hold its master key from that moment on, and a 58 standard ATProtocol server has no way to accept that — it can only create 59 accounts where the server holds the key. If you point Obsign at another server, 60 it says so on the server screen, before you fill anything in, and offers to 61 import an identity there instead. 62 ::: 63 64 ## Import an identity 65 66 If you already have an ATProtocol identity — on [bsky.social](https://bsky.social), 67 a self-hosted PDS, anywhere — choose **I have an account somewhere**. Obsign installs this 68 device's key as the identity's master key, which is what unlocks tamper 69 monitoring, the 72-hour reversal window, and your own backups. The account itself 70 does not move: it keeps running on the same server, with the same handle. 71 72 Importing works against any spec-compliant server, Custos or not. 73 74 Moving the account to a different server is a separate decision you can make 75 later, from the identity's own screen: [Migrating your 76 identity](/user/migration/). 77 78 ## Advanced: anchor to a domain you control (did:web) 79 80 By default, a new identity is a **did:plc** — an entry in ATProtocol's public 81 PLC directory. That is the right choice for almost everyone, and everything 82 else in these docs assumes it. 83 84 If you already run a domain, Obsign also offers **did:web**: your identity 85 becomes `did:web:your-domain.example`, anchored to a DID document served from 86 that domain rather than to the PLC directory. The wallet walks you through 87 composing the document, proves you control the domain by requiring the exact 88 reviewed document to be live at its authoritative HTTPS URL before the server 89 accepts it, and can either let your server host the document for you or leave 90 you hosting it yourself. 91 92 The trade is real, which is why it sits behind an "Advanced" link: 93 94 - **You gain** an identity rooted in something you already own. No directory, 95 and no server, sits between you and it. 96 - **You take on** the domain as part of your security perimeter. A did:web 97 identity has no PLC rotation keys, so the 98 [tamper monitoring and 72-hour override](/user/recovery/) and the 99 [2-of-3 share backup](/user/backup/) do not apply — recovery is controlling 100 the domain (plus your device key), and losing the domain means losing the 101 identity. 102 103 ## The custody model, briefly 104 105 Your identity is anchored by rotation keys, in order of precedence: 106 107 - `rotationKeys[0]` — **yours**, held by Obsign on your device. 108 - `rotationKeys[1]` — your **recovery key**, derived from the secret your 109 [2-of-3 Shamir backup](/user/backup/) protects. Your device creates it; the 110 server never sees it. 111 - `rotationKeys[2]` — the server's, used only for routine operations. 112 113 You can see them on an identity's DID document screen — `#rotation-0` is your 114 device key, and the server's key always sits last. 115 116 120 121 Because your key outranks the server's, you can always override the server. That 122 ordering is what makes _credible exit_ a property of the keys, not a promise. 123

1	// pattern: Imperative Shell
2	//
3	//! `repo_seq` firehose event-log retention.
4	//!
5	//! A periodic background task that prunes the durable firehose event log (`repo_seq`, added by
6	//! V028) so it does not grow without bound. Every `#commit` and `#account` frame — including each
7	//! commit's CARv1 `blocks` — is retained in `repo_seq` so `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos` cursor
8	//! replay survives restarts (see `firehose.rs`). Without a sweep the table is append-only and
9	//! would eventually dominate the production SQLite DB and the Litestream backup.
10	//!
11	//! ## Policy (union — the most aggressive enabled retention bounds growth)
12	//!
13	//! On each pass the sweep computes a **low-water mark** below which rows are prunable, from the
14	//! enabled retention knobs (see [`FirehoseConfig`](common::FirehoseConfig)):
15	//!
16	//! * **Age** (`log_retention_secs`): rows whose `sequenced_at` is older than `now − retention`
17	//!   are prunable. The age watermark is `first_retained_seq − 1`, where `first_retained_seq` is
18	//!   `MIN(seq)` among rows *at or after* the cutoff (see [`firehose_seq::retained_boundary_seq`]);
19	//!   if no row is retained by age, the whole log is prunable up to the frontier.
20	//! * **Count** (`log_retention_count`): keep at most the newest `N` rows, i.e. the watermark is
21	//!   `MAX(seq) − N`.
22	//!
23	//! The combined watermark is the **`max`** of the enabled policies' contributions: a row is
24	//! pruned when it falls below **any** enabled cutoff, so enabling both knobs bounds growth by
25	//! whichever policy fires (age prunes old rows even when count would keep them; count prunes a
26	//! huge young backlog even when age would keep it). A `0` knob disables that policy and
27	//! contributes nothing; both at `0` makes the sweep a no-op (the log stays append-only, exactly
28	//! the pre-retention behaviour).
29	//!
30	//! The age boundary is deliberately computed from the first *retained* seq rather than
31	//! `MAX(seq)` among old rows, so a row with a skewed-old timestamp can never lift the watermark
32	//! past fresh rows (an over-prune / data loss). The worst case under non-monotonic timestamps is
33	//! that an oddly-timestamped row lingers — an under-prune the next pass corrects.
34	//!
35	//! ## Invariants preserved
36	//!
37	//! * **The live frontier is never pruned.** The watermark is clamped to `MAX(seq) − 1`, so a
38	//!   reconnecting relay can always resume from at least the newest retained event and `read_replay`
39	//!   can always reach the frontier it snapshotted.
40	//! * **`seq` stays monotonic and is never reused.** `seq` is the explicit `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`,
41	//!   so a pruned number is gone for good; the sequencer keeps advancing from its in-memory
42	//!   `last_seq` regardless of what was pruned below it.
43	//! * **The retained suffix stays dense.** Pruning removes a contiguous prefix `seq ≤ watermark`,
44	//!   so the remaining `watermark+1 .. MAX(seq)` range has no holes and `read_replay`'s per-row
45	//!   density check still holds within it. A cursor below the pruned window degrades to
46	//!   best-effort replay (the subscriber receives the retained suffix) rather than failing closed.
47	//!
48	//! Like the blob GC it is best-effort, runs for the life of the process, and is dropped on
49	//! shutdown rather than joined.

39	/// respects the inter-child foreign keys (**no account-keyed FK cascades**: the schema's only
40	/// `ON DELETE CASCADE`s hang content-addressed ownership rows off their physical tables
41	/// (`block_owners.cid` → `blocks`, `blob_owners.cid` → `blobs`), never off `accounts`, so every
42	/// child must be deleted explicitly and in dependency order before the `accounts` row):
43	///
44	/// * `refresh_tokens` before `sessions` (`refresh_tokens.session_id → sessions.id`)
45	/// * `transfer_audit_events` before `transfers` before `transfer_devices`
46	///   (`transfer_audit_events.transfer_id → transfers.id`, `transfers.accepted_device_id →
47	///   transfer_devices.id`)
48	/// * `agent_audit_events` and `agent_claim_attempts` before `agent_identities`
49	///   (`agent_audit_events.registration_id → agent_identities.id`,
50	///   `agent_claim_attempts.identity_id → agent_identities.id`); audit events are keyed through
51	///   the identity rather than their own `did` column because pre-claim events on an anonymous
52	///   registration carry a NULL `did` but still pin the identity row via the FK. Any audit event
53	///   left carrying this DID on a *foreign* account's registration is part of that account's
54	///   trail, so it is unlinked (`did = NULL` — the column is nullable) rather than deleted.
55	/// * `sovereign_session_nonces` before `accounts` (each replay row is FK-owned by its DID)
56	/// * `email_tokens` before `accounts` (FK-owned by the DID; consumption only stamps `used_at`,
57	///   so confirm/update rows persist for the account's lifetime and must be purged here)
58	/// * `recovery_otps`, `recovery_audit_events`, and `recovery_escrow` before `accounts` (all
59	///   FK-owned by the DID; no FK links them, so their relative order is free)
60	///
61	/// The sovereign-child-agent tables (V047/V049) are scoped by *both* of their DID columns:
62	///
63	/// * `agent_identities` / `agent_child_provisionings` are additionally keyed
64	///   `WHERE parent_did = ?`: a purged parent's children lose the account their custody chains to
65	///   (ADR-0023), so their registration/provisioning rows go with the parent — the child
66	///   *accounts* are cascade-scheduled for the reaper by `purge_account` itself (see below).
67	/// * `agent_child_provisionings` is keyed `WHERE child_did = ?`: a minted child's provisioning row
68	///   FK-references `accounts(did)` on `child_did`, so deleting a child account without first
69	///   removing this row is a foreign-key violation. A no-op for a non-child account (only children
70	///   have a provisioning row).
71	/// * `agent_child_deletions` is keyed `WHERE parent_did = ?` — never `child_did`. It is the durable
72	///   child-deletion tombstone that must *survive* a child's purge to keep the parent's audit view
73	///   alive, so it carries no FK on `child_did`; it is anchored to `parent_did` and reclaimed only
74	///   when the *parent* is deleted. A no-op for a child (a child authors no deletions).
75	///
76	/// The `purge_covers_every_account_foreign_key_in_the_schema` test walks the live schema's
77	/// FK graph and fails if a migration adds an account-keyed table this list doesn't reach.
78	///
79	/// `did_documents` and `reserved_signing_keys` carry the DID with no FK to `accounts`, but are
80	/// scoped by `did` so removing this account's rows is correct. `repo_seq` (the durable firehose
81	/// log) is deliberately **excluded**: it is a shared, densely-sequenced log and punching per-DID
82	/// holes in it would break cursor-replay's density invariant for every other account. The
83	/// account's history there ages out via the normal retention sweep; the `#account` (deleted) frame
84	/// we emit is how subscribers learn the account is gone.
85	const DELETE_BY_DID: &[&str] = &[
86	    "DELETE FROM account_labels WHERE did = ?",
87	    "DELETE FROM operator_account_audit_events WHERE did = ?",
88	    "DELETE FROM refresh_tokens WHERE did = ?",
89	    "DELETE FROM sessions WHERE did = ?",

# PDS Crate (Custos)

Last verified: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

The PDS is the axum-based web server. It is the sole Imperative Shell in the workspace —
the only crate that touches SQLite, handles HTTP, or manages process-level state. All other
crates (`crypto`, `repo-engine`, `common`) are pure Functional Cores that the PDS calls.

## Module Map

```
src/
  main.rs          — startup: open pool, run migrations, bind server
  telemetry.rs     — OTel tracing-subscriber init (`init_subscriber`) + shutdown-flushing `OtelGuard`; wired by main.rs at startup, dropped after graceful shutdown. `[telemetry] log_format = "json"` switches the stdout fmt layer to one-JSON-object-per-line
  metrics.rs       — OTel meter + Prometheus registry behind `GET /metrics` (see "Metrics" section below): typed `Metrics` handle in AppState, instrument/label name constants (`metrics::names`), the `http_requests_total` middleware, and the `SubscriberGuard` RAII gauge
  app.rs           — router construction (route table + shared middleware layers); re-exports `AppState`/`FailedLoginStore` (and, under `#[cfg(test)]`, `test_state`/`test_state_with_plc_url`) from `state.rs` so the ~120 existing `crate::app::AppState` imports across the crate stay unchanged
  state.rs         — `AppState` definition + `FailedLoginStore`, plus the `#[cfg(test)]` `test_state`/`test_state_with_plc_url` constructors
  xrpc_dispatch.rs — the catch-all XRPC proxy dispatcher (`xrpc_handler`, registered by `app.rs` at `/xrpc/{method}`): resolves `app.bsky.*`/`chat.bsky.*`/`com.atproto.moderation.*` to an upstream (configured default or an `atproto-proxy`-header target), enforces the read-after-write munge branch, and records `proxy_requests_total`
  firehose/        — persistent subscribeRepos event pipeline (durable sequencer + broadcast fan-out)
  firehose_gc.rs   — periodic `repo_seq` retention sweep (age/count pruning below the live frontier)
  blob_store.rs    — blob storage backend: filesystem I/O, CID computation, MIME-type detection; blobs live at `{data_dir}/blobs/{cid[0:2]}/{cid}`
  blob_gc.rs       — periodic blob GC over per-account ownership rows (`blob_owners`, V039): reconciles each account's MST-referenced blobs into its ownership rows (permanent vs released-with-grace, adopting referenced-but-unowned stored CIDs), then sweeps expired unreferenced rows — the shared physical row + file are deleted only when the last owner is gone. The sweep **fails closed on a failed reconcile**: an account whose repo walk errored this pass is excluded from it by DID, because its `temp_until` pins were never cleared and the global sweep cannot otherwise tell "references nothing" from "references unknown". Such an account leaks disk until the fault is fixed, and is reported via `blob_gc_errors_total` + the sweep snapshot's `errors`
  blob_mirror/     — off-volume blob replication to an S3-compatible bucket (`[blob_mirror]` / `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_*`, the Litestream analogue for blob files, which Litestream never covers): `mod.rs` is the periodic sweep (template: blob_gc.rs — upload verified-missing keys, propagate row deletions on a harmless lag, with a tripwire refusing delete propagation when the `blobs` table is empty against a non-empty bucket) plus `restore_missing_blobs`, run by main.rs *before the listener binds* so a Litestream-restored DB is reconciled with the blob directory before anything is served; `s3.rs` is a minimal hand-rolled SigV4 client (put/get/delete/ListObjectsV2, signing pinned against the AWS documentation's worked examples). Both mirror directions re-hash bytes against their CID (`blob_store::compute_cid`) before trusting them: a corrupt local file never becomes the recovery copy, and a corrupt bucket copy is never materialised at a valid CID path. `BlobMirror::fetch_verified` (fetch + verify one CID) is the shared entry point `blob_scrub.rs`'s auto-heal reuses. `test_support.rs` (`#[cfg(test)]`) holds the shared fake-S3 test double + `BlobMirror` builder both this module's and `blob_scrub.rs`'s tests use
  blob_scrub.rs    — periodic blob-integrity scrub sweep (`[blob_scrub]` / `EZPDS_BLOB_SCRUB_*`, template: blob_gc.rs, same failed-pass-leaves-timestamp-stale posture): re-hashes every stored blob's file against its `blobs` row (hash + size) and walks the blob directory for both orphan directions nothing else scans for — a row whose file is missing (the migration-blocking fault) and a file no row owns (a leak `blob_gc` never sees, since it only ever works from DB rows outward). When `[blob_mirror]` is configured and `auto_heal` is on, a bad/missing file is repaired from the bucket's verified copy (`BlobMirror::fetch_verified`, written back through `blob_store::store_blob`'s durable temp-file+fsync+rename path so a healed file is exactly as crash-durable as a fresh upload); otherwise the problem is only ever flagged, converting silent rot into an operator signal
  crawler.rs       — outbound requestCrawl notifier (rate-limited, retrying, fire-and-forget)
  relay_status.rs  — inbound `com.atproto.sync.getHostStatus` client: asks the upstream relay what it knows about this PDS (its cursor into our seq-space, indexed-account count, lifecycle status), total/never-fatal (every failure is a `RelayReport` variant). Backs `GET /v1/admin/relay-status`
  email.rs         — pluggable outbound email sender (`Arc<dyn EmailSender>` in AppState): `LogEmailSender` (default; logs instead of sending — keeps tests/fresh installs offline) + `SmtpEmailSender` (real delivery via `lettre`, rustls) + `HttpEmailSender` (real delivery via Mailtrap's transactional HTTPS Send API over `reqwest`, `provider = "mailtrap"`; needs only outbound HTTPS, so it works where outbound SMTP ports are blocked — e.g. Railway's non-Pro plans). Backs the password-reset / email-confirmation / email-update / PLC-op / account-delete token deliveries. Configured by `[email]` in `pds.toml` / `EZPDS_EMAIL_*` (Mailtrap: `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TOKEN`, optional `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_API_URL` / `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECS`)
  rate_limit.rs    — request rate-limiting middleware + shared limiter state (global IP, per-endpoint IP, per-account write points)
  iroh_tunnel.rs   — Iroh QUIC endpoint: NAT-traversing device↔pds tunnel (opt-in)
  notify_relay_client.rs — the pds's first *outbound* iroh leg: dials the configured notification relay (`ezpds/notify/0`) from the same `IrohState` endpoint `iroh_tunnel.rs` accepts on, so the instance presents one node identity — which is exactly the identity the relay authorizes (`connection.remote_id()`; no credential travels in a message). One JSON request per bidi stream, lazily-dialed cached connection with a one-shot re-dial retry (the expected failure is a *stale* connection after a relay restart), and enroll-on-`notEnrolled` rather than a startup step, so a relay that is restarted or reached first mid-run heals by itself. Also owns the fire-and-forget send worker: triggers enqueue `NotifyJob`s onto an unbounded in-process mpsc and return immediately, because a trigger that blocks on a push relay has traded a missed banner for a broken request. In-memory only, deliberately — a missed push is a missed *banner*, not lost data (the app reconciles from Custos), so durable queuing would add a table, a sweep, and a retry policy to protect something already recoverable. The worker writes back relay handles and prunes a registration the relay reports `unregistered` (APNs 410)
  notifications.rs — the sending side: `notify_device(state, did, payload)` / `notify_admin_devices` load the registrations, load the active sender key once per fan-out, then **pad and seal once per device** (HPKE seals to a single recipient; reusing an encapsulated key across devices would be a weaker protocol) and enqueue. Padding is computed against the *serialized APNs body* — the only length an observer measures — via the shared `notify_relay::protocol::apns_envelope`, so the sender's arithmetic and the relay's serialization cannot disagree. A payload too large for the top bucket is **dropped**, not sent unpadded or truncated: sending it would leak the exact length padding exists to hide. Sender keys are generated lazily (first send, or first `sender-keys` fetch — an app must be able to pin a key before the first notification arrives). Nothing here is fallible from a caller's perspective; every path ends in an enqueue or a log line.
