content.content:
1	---
2	title: Master-key disaster runbook
3	description: What to do if the KEK is lost or compromised — the incident procedure for operators.
4	---
5	
6	`EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` is the key-encryption key (KEK): a 32-byte
7	AES-256-GCM key, supplied env-only, that wraps every at-rest secret in the PDS
8	database — most importantly each account's repo signing key, the one that
9	signs every commit. See [Configuration](/operator/configuration/) for how it's
10	provisioned and rotated day to day. This page is the incident checklist for
11	when something goes wrong with it.
12	
13	## What the key protects
14	
15	| Secret | Self-heals? | Recovery if the KEK is gone |
16	| --- | --- | --- |
17	| Per-account repo signing keys | No | **Hard** — wallet-driven rotation |
18	| Operator-level (legacy) commit-signing keys | No | **Hard** — same path |
19	| OAuth signing key, JWT secret, Iroh node key | Yes | Drop the row; re-mints on boot |
20	| PDS-held Shamir recovery share (Share 2 of 3) | No | **Hard** — needs the original KEK |
21	
22	The three self-healing secrets cost little to lose: delete the row and the
23	server mints a fresh one under the current KEK on next boot (sessions
24	re-auth; the Iroh node id changes and devices re-resolve it). **The
25	commit-signing keys are the entire difficulty** in both scenarios below,
26	because each one is published in an account's DID document and can only be
27	replaced by a PLC operation signed by a *current* rotation key — the PDS
28	cannot silently swap one out from under a user.
29	
30	## Golden rule (prevention)
31	
32	**Back up the KEK as carefully as the database, and store it separately from
33	the DB backup.** A KEK backed up next to your [Litestream replica](/operator/backups/)
34	gives an attacker who reaches that one location both halves — the ciphertext
35	and the key that decrypts it — which defeats at-rest encryption entirely.
36	Store the KEK in a secrets manager or offline vault distinct from where the
37	database backup lives. This single practice turns Scenario 1 below from
38	catastrophic into a non-event.
39	
40	---
41	
42	## Scenario 1 — KEK lost (never exposed)
43	
44	**Symptom:** after a redeploy or environment change, the server won't boot —
45	it hard-errors that encrypted material exists in the database but the key to
46	decrypt it is gone.
47	
48	### 1.1 First: is it actually lost?
49	
50	Check the secrets manager or vault backup (per the golden rule). If the KEK
51	is recoverable, restore the environment variable and boot normally — **stop
52	here**, this is a misplaced env var, not a disaster. Only proceed if the KEK
53	is genuinely unrecoverable.
54	
55	### 1.2 If genuinely lost
56	
57	1. **Set a fresh KEK.**
58	2. **Self-healing secrets** — with the database and the new KEK in place,
59	   delete the OAuth signing key, JWT secret, and Iroh identity rows and boot.
60	   Each regenerates under the new KEK automatically.
61	3. **Commit-signing keys — permanently undecryptable.** The old ciphertext
62	   can no longer be read, so the server can no longer sign commits under the
63	   published verification method. There is no server-side fix. Each affected
64	   account must go through **wallet-driven repo-key rotation**
65	   (`POST /v1/repo-keys/rotation` + `/complete`): the server generates a fresh
66	   repo key, the account's wallet signs a PLC operation repointing the
67	   signing verification method and the server's rotation key, and the server
68	   cuts over. Prioritize active accounts.
69	4. **Escrowed Shamir shares — also permanently undecryptable.** There is no
70	   server-side re-mint, because a replacement wouldn't be one of the shares
71	   already issued to the user. Recovery must fall back to the user's other
72	   two shares.
73	
74	:::note[Takeaway]
75	A lost KEK is nearly as bad as a compromised one, purely because of the repo
76	keys — loss and compromise share the same hard recovery path (per-account
77	wallet-driven rotation).
78	:::
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Scenario 2 — KEK compromised (assume the DB was exposed too)
83	
84	**Threat assumption:** if the KEK leaked, assume the attacker also has, or
85	can get, a copy of the database. Treat every KEK-wrapped secret as
86	plaintext-known to the attacker. Re-wrapping under a new KEK is necessary
87	hygiene but does **not** by itself contain the compromise — the underlying
88	keys must be rotated too, not just re-encrypted.
89	
90	### 2.1 Contain the environment-variable blast radius first
91	
92	Whatever exposed the KEK (leaked deployment variables, dashboard access, a
93	leaked deploy log) almost certainly exposed the other env secrets. Rotate
94	all of them, most-urgent first:
95	
96	1. **`EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN`** — the break-glass bearer credential; rotate
97	   immediately, it gates admin, moderation, and device routes.
98	2. SMTP / mail-provider tokens.
99	3. Any other deployment secrets in the same store.
100	4. Investigate the exposure vector and revoke the access path (rotate
101	   deployment-platform credentials, audit who or what could read the
102	   environment).
103	
104	### 2.2 New KEK, then re-wrap
105	
106	Generate a fresh KEK. Use the offline `pds rewrap-master-key` subcommand
107	(see [Configuration](/operator/configuration/)) to re-encrypt the surviving
108	blobs under it, then drop and re-mint the self-healing secrets (next step).
109	This protects the database at rest under a key the attacker doesn't have,
110	going forward.
111	
112	### 2.3 Rotate the self-healing secrets
113	
114	Delete the OAuth signing key, JWT secret, and Iroh identity rows and let the
115	server re-mint them under the new KEK on boot. This invalidates any
116	access/refresh tokens the attacker could have forged with the leaked keys —
117	users re-auth, devices re-resolve the node id.
118	
119	### 2.4 Rotate the commit-signing keys — the hard part
120	
121	The server **cannot** do this unilaterally: doing so would require signing
122	the rotation with the very key that's compromised. Recovery is
123	wallet-driven and per-account — the user's wallet holds the
124	higher-precedence rotation key and signs a PLC operation rotating the
125	signing verification method and the server's rotation key to a fresh
126	server-generated one, via `POST /v1/repo-keys/rotation`. Prioritize active
127	accounts; for a mass event, each wallet must still sign individually.
128	
129	A malicious party holding the compromised server-side rotation key can sign
130	bad commits and lower-priority PLC operations, but **cannot** move the
131	identity away from the user — the wallet's higher-precedence key outranks it
132	and can override within the identity directory's recovery window. The repo
133	is self-certifying, so the identity itself is never lost; the commit-signing
134	key is what must be rotated.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## Quick reference — ordering
139	
140	**Loss:** verify backup → (if recoverable) restore & boot, done → else: new KEK →
141	drop + re-mint easy secrets → per-account wallet-driven repo-key rotation.
142	
143	**Compromise:** rotate `EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN` + mail tokens + env access → new KEK +
144	`pds rewrap-master-key` → drop + re-mint easy secrets → per-account wallet-driven
145	repo-key rotation.
146	
147	---
148	
149	:::note[Looking for source-level detail?]
150	This page is the operator-facing procedure. The engineering version — table
151	and migration names, source file references, and the escrow-share model in
152	full — lives in the repository at
153	[`docs/operations/master-key-disaster-runbook.md`](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/blob/main/docs/operations/master-key-disaster-runbook.md).
154	The golden rule and the quick-reference ordering above are kept identical
155	between the two copies; `just runbook-parity-check` fails CI if they drift.
156	:::

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	set -euo pipefail
3	
4	cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
5	node scripts/runbook-parity-check.mjs
6

1	---
2	title: Capabilities
3	description: What your deployment advertises to clients, what each capability means, and how you control it.
4	---
5	
6	Custos tells clients what it can do. `com.atproto.server.describeServer` — the
7	public, unauthenticated endpoint every AT Protocol client already calls — carries
8	an extra `custos` object alongside the standard fields:
9	
10	```json
11	{
12	  "did": "did:web:pds.example.com",
13	  "availableUserDomains": ["example.com"],
14	  "inviteCodeRequired": true,
15	  "phoneVerificationRequired": false,
16	  "custos": {
17	    "version": "0.8.1",
18	    "capabilities": ["sovereignSessions", "walletConsent", "walletAccountDelete", "didWebHosting"]
19	  }
20	}
21	```
22	
23	A client reads `capabilities` and enables the matching features. Obsign, for
24	example, only offers to create a brand-new identity on a server that advertises
25	`createCeremony`, and only offers escrow-assisted recovery where `escrow` is
26	advertised — instead of calling the endpoint and interpreting the failure.
27	
28	Two properties follow from this being a **list of named capabilities rather than
29	an "is this Custos?" flag**. First, your deployment is described by what it
30	actually offers: a Custos server running without a master key advertises fewer
31	capabilities, and clients adapt rather than break. Second, a server that sends no
32	`custos` object at all — the reference PDS, rsky-pds, millipds — simply has none
33	of these, and a well-behaved client falls back to standard AT Protocol behaviour.
34	Nothing here is required of anyone; the extension is additive, and clients that
35	do not know the field ignore it.
36	
37	The complete, generated list lives in the
38	[capability reference](/operator/reference/capabilities/). This page explains what
39	each capability means for you and how to switch it on.
40	
41	## Identifying your server
42	
43	`GET /xrpc/_health` reports a self-identifying version string rather than a bare
44	number:
45	
46	```json
47	{ "version": "custos v0.8.1", "db": "ok" }
48	```
49	
50	This is the shape third-party AT Protocol diagnostic tooling reads to fingerprint
51	an implementation (millipds reports `millipds v…` the same way; the reference PDS
52	returns a bare commit hash that names no software). It is also what Obsign pings
53	when you point it at a server. Nothing in it is sensitive: it names software and
54	version, which any protocol-level probe can already infer.
55	
56	## The capabilities
57	
58	Each heading below is the literal name that appears in `custos.capabilities`.
59	
60	### `createCeremony`
61	
62	Custos-native identity creation: mobile signup, per-account repo signing key
63	issuance, and the client-authored `did:plc` genesis ceremony in which the user's
64	device key is written into the DID's rotation keys from the very first operation.
65	This is the only way an identity is born already sovereign — the standard
66	`createAccount` lexicon never lets a client author its own genesis rotation keys.
67	
68	Without it, a wallet steers users to *import* an existing identity instead, and
69	the claim ceremony takes sovereign custody of an identity hosted anywhere.
70	
71	**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The ceremony issues each account a
72	repo signing key and stores it encrypted under the master key, so a deployment
73	with no `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` cannot perform it and does not advertise
74	it. There is no separate switch: configure a master key (as any real deployment
75	should — see [Configuration](/operator/configuration/)) and the capability
76	appears.
77	
78	### `escrow`
79	
80	Custos holds one share of the account's 2-of-3 Shamir recovery split — encrypted,
81	and useless on its own — and releases it through the recovery gate: an emailed
82	one-time code, then a cancellable delay window during which the account holder is
83	notified and can abort. This is what makes recovery possible for a user who has
84	lost their device but still holds one share.
85	
86	Without it, the wallet's recovery story is entirely self-held: the user keeps
87	both remaining shares themselves, and no server is involved in recovery at all.
88	
89	**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The stored share envelope is
90	encrypted under the master key, so a deployment without one cannot accept a
91	deposit or perform a release, and does not advertise the capability. The delay
92	window itself is tuned separately with `recovery.release_delay_secs`
93	(`EZPDS_RECOVERY_RELEASE_DELAY_SECS`, default 24 hours) — that changes how a
94	release behaves, not whether escrow is offered.
95	
96	### `sovereignSessions`
97	
98	Passwordless full-access sessions. Instead of a password, the client signs a
99	fresh, timestamped, nonce-bound proof with a key that is already in the
100	identity's current PLC rotation keys, and Custos verifies it against
101	plc.directory — never against a cached document. The account holder's device key
102	*is* the credential, so an account can have no password at all.
103	
104	Everything that needs a full-access session rides on this: app passwords,
105	changing a handle, removing an identity, restoring media from a backup.
106	
107	**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
108	switch. It grants Custos no additional power over an identity — any current
109	rotation key qualifies, and rotation keys are the account holder's to control.
110	
111	### `agents`
112	
113	The [auth.md](https://github.com/workos/auth.md) agent surface: an AI agent or
114	automation registers with the server, the account holder confirms the claim from
115	their wallet (reading the exact scopes first), and the agent then exchanges its
116	assertion for narrowly-scoped, revocable, audited access tokens. Agent tokens can
117	never manage agents — including themselves — and every registration is revocable
118	from the wallet or by the identity provider.
119	
120	**Controlled by:** `agent_auth.service_auth_enabled`,
121	`agent_auth.anonymous_enabled`, `agent_auth.trusted_issuers`. These are the three
122	ways an agent can register, and **all three are off or empty by default** — an
123	untouched deployment does not offer agents at all. Enable whichever registration
124	flows you want (`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_SERVICE_AUTH_ENABLED`,
125	`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED`, or a configured `[[agent_auth.trusted_issuers]]`
126	entry) and the capability appears. What a claimed agent may then do is bounded
127	separately by `agent_auth.granted_scopes`; narrowing it narrows every assertion
128	minted afterwards.
129	
130	### `walletConsent`
131	
132	An OAuth authorization can be approved in the identity wallet with a
133	device-key-signed decision, rather than by typing a password into a browser
134	consent page. The signed envelope binds the request, the client, the decision,
135	and the exact scope set, so an approval cannot be replayed onto a different
136	request, flipped from a denial, or widened after the fact.
137	
138	**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
139	switch. Password-based browser consent continues to work for accounts that have a
140	password; the wallet path is an additional, stronger route to the same grant.
141	
142	### `optionalPassword`
143	
144	An account can be created on this server with no password at all. A client that
145	sees this capability may omit the password field entirely when creating an
146	account; the account is stored with no password hash and authenticates
147	afterwards through its device key — wallet-confirmed OAuth consent and sovereign
148	sessions — plus app passwords for standard AT Protocol clients like the Bluesky
149	app.
150	
151	Passwordless accounts are not a new storage shape: accounts that migrate in from
152	another server have always been stored without a password. What this capability
153	changes is only whether a *new* account may be created that way.
154	
155	An **empty** password is refused whether or not this is enabled, and that is
156	deliberate: an empty string is what an uninitialised form field sends, so
157	accepting one would let a client bug create an account with no credential that
158	nobody asked for. Omitting the field is the only way to ask.
159	
160	**Controlled by:** `accounts.password_optional`. Off by default — a passwordless
161	account depends on device-key custody you cannot verify on the account holder's
162	behalf, so a deployment whose users are not all running the identity wallet
163	should keep the password required. Enable it with `[accounts] password_optional =
164	true` (`EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`) and the capability appears. Turning it
165	back off stops new passwordless accounts being created; it does not affect
166	accounts that already have no password, which keep working exactly as before.
167	
168	### `walletAccountDelete`
169	
170	An account can be permanently deleted with a device-key-signed proof from one of
171	its current rotation keys, in place of the account password. The emailed
172	single-use confirmation code is still required — this swaps one of the two
173	factors, it does not remove one.
174	
175	This capability is what makes `optionalPassword` safe to turn on. Deletion is the
176	one operation that had no route around the password: an account created without
177	one could be made, used, and migrated, but never removed, because every
178	credential path answered with the same refusal and left the holder no way
179	forward. The proof closes that.
180	
181	The signed envelope binds this server, the account, the signing key, the moment,
182	and a single-use nonce, and it is verified against the identity's **authoritative**
183	current rotation set read live from plc.directory — never a cached document. It is
184	accepted for accounts that *do* have a password too: a current rotation key can
185	already migrate or retire the identity outright, so it is the stronger credential,
186	and honouring only the weaker one would make the endpoint answer differently
187	depending on whether a password exists. Unknown accounts, wrong passwords, and bad
188	proofs remain one indistinguishable response.
189	
190	**Controlled by:** always. This is the same key-sovereign trust model as
191	`sovereignSessions` and has no operator switch; password-based deletion continues
192	to work unchanged for accounts that have a password.
193	
194	### `didWebHosting`
195	
196	Custos serves an opted-in account's `did:web` document at the account's own
197	domain (`/.well-known/did.json`) and emits an identity event so relays re-resolve
198	after an edit.
199	
200	Hosting is opt-in **per account**, never automatic, and only ever for a domain
201	the user controls: moving the document onto Custos trades away some of the
202	independence a self-hosted document gives an identity, so it is the account
203	holder's decision. Exit is a DNS repoint away.
204	
205	**Controlled by:** always. The server-side capability is inherent to running
206	Custos and has no operator switch; whether any given account uses it is that
207	account holder's choice.
208	
209	### `waitlist`
210	
211	A public interest-signup waitlist for a pre-launch deployment: an unauthenticated
212	`POST /waitlist` accepting an email address plus an optional atproto handle, meant
213	to be posted to directly from a marketing page on another origin (the endpoint is
214	CORS-open and carries no credentials). Signups are idempotent per email — a repeat
215	returns the same success and never discloses whether an address was already on the
216	list — and the handle is syntax-checked but deliberately never resolved, so the
217	endpoint has no outbound-request surface. The operator reads the list back with
218	`GET /v1/admin/waitlist` (newest first, with a total), which keeps working even
219	after the public endpoint is switched off again.
220	
221	**Controlled by:** `waitlist.enabled`. Off by default — an instance that isn't
222	running a launch funnel should not carry a public write endpoint it never asked
223	for. Enable it with `[waitlist] enabled = true` (`EZPDS_WAITLIST_ENABLED`) and the
224	capability appears; the per-IP signup rate cap is `rate_limit.waitlist_per_5min`
225	(`EZPDS_RATE_LIMIT_WAITLIST_PER_5MIN`, default 30).
226	
227	## Keeping this page honest
228	
229	The capability table in the server source
230	(`crates/pds/src/capabilities.rs`) is the single source of truth: it holds each
231	capability's wire name, the configuration that gates it, and the predicate the
232	server actually evaluates. The
233	[capability reference](/operator/reference/capabilities/) is generated from it,
234	and a CI gate (`just capability-docs-check`) fails the build if a capability is
235	added, renamed, or re-gated without this page being updated in the same change.
236	If a "Controlled by" line above disagrees with your server's behaviour, that is a
237	bug, not a documentation lag — please report it.
238

1 --- 2 title: Running a relay 3 description: Stand up the PDS, check its health, and understand what you are responsible for. 4 --- 5 6 The PDS is a single Rust binary with a SQLite database. It is designed to be 7 easy to host — the whole point of the project. 8 9 ## Health 10 11 Every deployment exposes a health endpoint the platform can watch: 12 13 ```sh 14 curl -sS https://your-pds.example.com/xrpc/_health 15 ``` 16 17 A healthy server reports its version, derived from the workspace version — the 18 same source these docs stamp — so the server and its documentation cannot claim 19 different versions. 20 21 :::note[Status is stated, not colored] 22 The operator console reports raw facts — version, uptime, counts, sweep 23 last-runs — and draws no `healthy`/`degraded`/`down` verdict of its own: the 24 thresholds are the operator's judgment, not the API's shape. What is wrong is 25 made legible in place — a troubled background sweep carries a trailing `!` glyph 26 and a named fault beside its figures, never a bare colored dot. A degraded 27 server tells you _what_ degraded. 28 ::: 29 30 34 35 On a degraded relay, the same readout flags each troubled background sweep with 36 a trailing `!` glyph and a named fault. A sweep whose last completed pass keeps 37 ageing reads `stale` — passes have stopped completing, so the sweep is dead. One 38 that completed but skipped work reads `failed ` — it ran, yet recorded `n` 39 errors (for blob GC, an account whose reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs 40 stay uncollected until the fault is fixed). The two are named so they read apart on a 41 row that has both, and _what_ degraded is legible without relying on color. 42 43 47 48 ## Is the upstream relay seeing you? 49 50 A healthy server that no relay is crawling is invisible to the network — and an 51 upstream relay can silently drop your subscription. The console's Home screen 52 carries a **Relay federation** block that compares your server's exact sequencer 53 head against what the upstream relay reports for your host: the relay's 54 lifecycle status, its cursor, how many events it is behind, and when it last 55 consumed one. **Request crawl** re-invites the relay on demand — the recovery 56 move when the readout says the relay has stopped listening. 57 58 62 63 The same facts are served at `GET /v1/admin/relay-status` and the re-invite at 64 `POST /v1/admin/request-crawl` — see the [API reference](/operator/reference/api/). 65 66 ## What you are responsible for 67 68 - **Durability** — the SQLite database is the identity store. Back it up. 69 Production streams continuous backups to object storage with Litestream — see 70 [Backups & restore](/operator/backups/). 71 - **Availability** — users' clients reach your server to read and write. Health 72 checks and restart policy are your safety net. 73 - **You can't lock anyone in** — you hold the lowest-precedence rotation key; 74 the user's device key (`rotationKeys[0]`) and their recovery key outrank it, 75 so they can move their identity to another server whenever they choose. Design 76 your operations for that. 77 78 :::caution[Do not treat the DB as disposable] 79 Losing the database is not like losing a cache. It holds the repositories your 80 users depend on. Verify your restore path before you need it. 81 ::: 82 83 ## Deploy 84 85 The server deploys as an OCI image (Railway builds the `Dockerfile` directly). 86 The full runbook — staging vs production branches, Litestream backups, and the 87 security posture — lives in the repository's `docs/deploy.md`. 88

content.content: 1 --- 2 title: Moderation 3 description: Takedown, restore, credential revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 4 --- 5 6 The operator console (the "Brass Console" companion app) exposes the moderation 7 actions an operator needs. Every action reports exactly what it did — the console 8 does not soften or hide the effect. 9 10 ## Actions 11 12 16 17 On the **Moderation** screen (look up an account by DID first): 18 19 - **Takedown** — stop serving an account: logins, writes, and sync are refused 20 until it is restored. 21 - **Restore** — reverse a takedown (the account resumes serving unless it is also 22 suspended or deactivated). 23 - **Credential revocation** — the incident-response follow-up for a compromised 24 account: in one sweep it revokes the account's **sessions, app passwords, OAuth 25 grants and pending authorization codes, and transfer-device tokens**, and reports 26 the literal per-family counts. The account's **main password is untouched**, and 27 any already-issued access tokens lapse on their own within minutes. Every holder 28 — including the owner — is signed out and must log in again. 29 30 You reach an account by tapping it in the account list, which is searchable by 31 handle or DID and shows each account's blob quota. 32 33 37 38 On the **Account detail** screen (reached by tapping an account in the list): 39 40 - **Correct an email** — fix an account's email address; this resets it to 41 unconfirmed. 42 - **Issue a password-reset token** — mint a single-use, one-hour reset token for 43 out-of-band delivery. This is **refused for a passwordless / key-sovereign 44 account** — those recover through their escrowed key share, not a reset. 45 46 Both takedown and credential revocation are destructive, so the console arms them 47 behind a two-tap confirmation that restates the target, then a biometric gate, 48 before anything is signed. 49 50 :::caution[Takedown is server-scoped, not identity-scoped] 51 A takedown affects what _your_ server serves. Because the user holds 52 `rotationKeys[0]`, they can migrate their identity elsewhere. Moderation is your 53 control over your infrastructure, not custody over their identity — keep that 54 distinction clear when you communicate an action. 55 ::: 56 57 ## Labeler watching — flagged accounts 58 59 Custos can watch ATProto **labelers** (moderation services) and flag any hosted 60 account they label. Flagged accounts float to the top of the console's account 61 list with an explicit `⚑` indicator per label — the label value, the labeler, 62 and when it was applied — and the Home screen shows a flagged-accounts notice 63 for the active server. This turns the account list from a neutral roster into a 64 spam/abuse triage view: if a labeler your network trusts flags one of your 65 accounts, you see it on your next glance at the console. 66 67 Watching is **off by default** — you choose which labelers' judgment reorders 68 your console. The recommended starting point is Bluesky's moderation service: 69 70 ```bash 71 # Environment form: comma-separated labeler DIDs, each watching every label value. 72 EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED=did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac 73 ``` 74 75 or, in `pds.toml`, with an optional per-labeler watchlist (empty or omitted 76 `labels` means every label from that labeler counts): 77 78 ```toml 79 [labeler] 80 poll_interval_secs = 900 # default: 15 minutes 81 82 [[labeler.watched]] 83 did = "did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac" # Bluesky Moderation 84 labels = ["spam", "!hide", "!warn"] # omit to watch every label 85 86 [[labeler.watched]] 87 did = "did:web:some-other-labeler.example" # any labeler works, not just Bluesky's 88 ``` 89 90 How it works: a background pass polls each watched labeler's 91 `com.atproto.label.queryLabels` for your hosted accounts (the labeler's query 92 endpoint is resolved from its DID document), honoring label negations and 93 expiry, and reconciles the flagged state the console reads. The first pass runs 94 at startup, then every `poll_interval_secs`. The health readout reports the 95 watcher's last completed pass, so a stale pass is visible on the Status screen. 96 97 Two things worth knowing before you enable it: 98 99 - **Each poll discloses your hosted-account DIDs to the watched labeler** (they 100 arrive as the query's `uriPatterns`). Hosted DIDs are already publicly 101 enumerable via `com.atproto.sync.listRepos`, but watching a labeler does 102 establish a recurring outbound relationship with it — which is why this is an 103 explicit opt-in rather than a default. 104 - **A flag is the labeler's opinion, not a verdict.** Flagging changes only the 105 sort order and the indicator; it takes no action against the account. Takedown 106 and credential revocation remain your deliberate, gated decisions above. 107 108 Removing a labeler from the config (or disabling watching entirely) clears its 109 flags on the next pass or restart — flagged state never outlives the 110 configuration that produced it. 111 112 ## Accountability 113 114 Moderation actions are shown with their subject, the operator device that signed 115 them, and the result — status carried in text, not by color alone. Pair any 116 externally visible action with a clear, honest explanation to the affected user; 117 the tooling reports the literal truth, and so should you. 118 119 :::note[Per-device operator keys] 120 Operator actions are signed by a per-device key (Secure-Enclave-backed on real 121 devices). Revoking a device revokes its ability to act, per relay, without 122 disturbing the others. 123 ::: 124

2	title: Backups & restore
3	description: Continuous SQLite backups with Litestream, blob replication with the bucket mirror, integrity scrubbing, and how to restore.
4	---
5	
6	The PDS keeps its records in one SQLite database and its blobs (media files) on
7	the volume next to it, so backing those two things up **is** your
8	disaster-recovery plan. Custos uses [Litestream](https://litestream.io/) to
9	stream the database to object storage continuously and restore it on boot, and
10	its own **blob mirror** to do the same for blob files.
11	
12	## How it works
13	
14	When the Litestream environment variables are set, the container runs the PDS
15	under Litestream: it streams the SQLite write-ahead log to your bucket as writes
16	happen (not a nightly snapshot — a continuous replica), and on boot it restores
17	from that replica if the local database is missing. So a current restore point
18	always exists.
19	
20	The replica is defined in `litestream.yml` (committed in the repo) with
21	`force-path-style: false` — virtual-hosted-style addressing, which
22	Railway/Tigris-style buckets require.
23	
24	## Turning it on
25	
26	Set these on the environment you want backed up (production; staging and local
27	leave them unset and run the PDS directly):
28	
29	| Variable | Role |
30	| --- | --- |
31	| `LITESTREAM_S3_BUCKET` | The bucket the replica is written to. Setting this is what switches Litestream on. |
32	| `LITESTREAM_S3_ENDPOINT` | Object-storage endpoint (e.g. your Tigris/S3-compatible host). |
33	| `LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
34	| `LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
35	
36	:::caution[The bucket credentials are secrets]
37	Store them in your platform's secret manager, never in the repository or the
38	image — the same discipline as the [master key](/operator/configuration/). Anyone
39	with the replica has a full copy of your accounts' data.
40	:::
41	
42	:::caution[The replica is only half the picture]
43	This backup protects the *ciphertext*. It does **not** protect the
44	[master key](/operator/configuration/) that decrypts it — back that up
45	separately, in a different store than this replica. If the key is ever lost
46	or compromised, follow the [master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)
47	instead of restoring from here alone.
48	:::
49	
50	## Blobs: the bucket mirror
51	
52	Litestream replicates only the SQLite database. Uploaded blobs — avatars,
53	post images, video — live as files on the deployment volume, where losing the
54	volume would destroy every account's media. The blob mirror is the Litestream
55	analogue for those files: a periodic sweep uploads every stored blob to an
56	S3-compatible bucket, and on boot the server attempts to restore any file
57	missing from the volume out of the bucket **before it takes traffic**. The
58	restore is best-effort per blob: a blob whose bytes exist in neither place, or
59	whose bucket copy fails content-hash verification, is logged loudly (per-CID
60	error plus a boot summary count) and boot continues — that blob stays
61	unavailable rather than blocking startup.
62	
63	Turn it on by setting a bucket (unset means disabled):
64	
65	| Variable | Role |
66	| --- | --- |
67	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_BUCKET` | Bucket the mirror writes to. Setting this is what switches the mirror on. |
68	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ENDPOINT` | S3-compatible endpoint URL. |
69	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
70	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
71	
72	The sweep also propagates deletions, on a lag: after blob garbage collection or
73	account deletion removes a blob's database row, a subsequent sweep deletes the
74	bucket object, so the mirror tracks the live blobstore rather than growing
75	forever (the worst case of the lag is the bucket briefly retaining collected
76	blobs). As a tripwire against acting on a wrong or empty database, a sweep that
77	finds no blob rows at all while the bucket has objects skips delete propagation
78	entirely. The full knob list (region, path-style addressing,
79	key prefix, sweep interval) is in the
80	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
81	
82	:::note[Same discipline as the database replica]
83	Blob bytes are content-addressed but they are still your users' data — keep the
84	mirror bucket's credentials in your secret manager, exactly like the Litestream
85	bucket's.
86	:::
87	
88	## Blob integrity: the scrub sweep
89	
90	A backup only helps if the bytes it protects are still good. A periodic **scrub
91	sweep** re-hashes every stored blob against its recorded CID and size, and walks
92	the blob directory for orphans in both directions — a database row whose file has
93	gone missing, and a file that no row owns. Bitrot, a truncated write, or a bad
94	restore surfaces as an operator alarm (the `blob_scrub_*` metrics and
95	`GET /v1/admin/health`) **months before a migration would trip over it**, rather
96	than as a mystery at the worst possible moment.
97	
98	When the [bucket mirror](#blobs-the-bucket-mirror) is configured, the sweep can
99	do more than report: a file that fails its hash or has gone missing is
100	**auto-healed** from the mirror's verified-good copy. Auto-heal is on by default
101	and has no effect when the mirror is disabled — with no verified copy to pull
102	from, a bad file is only ever flagged, never silently replaced. Both knobs
103	(`blob_scrub.interval_secs`, default 6 hours; `blob_scrub.auto_heal`) are in the
104	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
105	
106	Two guarantees close the loop around the sweep, so it catches genuine bitrot
107	rather than gaps the write and read paths should have handled themselves:
108	
109	- **Writes are crash-durable.** An uploaded blob is written to a temp file,
110	  fsynced, atomically renamed onto its content-addressed path, and the directory
111	  fsynced, *before* the database row is recorded. A crash or power loss can no
112	  longer leave truncated bytes at a valid path behind a row that already
113	  committed.
114	- **Reads are verified.** `getBlob` re-hashes a blob against its CID before
115	  serving it and returns a 404 (flagging the scrub alarm counter) on a mismatch,
116	  so a corrupted file is never handed to a downstream cache. A verified response
117	  carries the long-lived `immutable` cache header the blob spec recommends.
118	
119	## Restoring
120	
121	To restore the database from the replica:
122	
123	```sh
124	litestream restore <path-to-db>
125	```
126	
127	Litestream pulls the latest state (or a point in time) from the bucket. On a
128	fresh container the PDS does this automatically on boot when the local database is
129	absent.
130	
131	### Rollback after a bad release
132	
133	Schema migrations are **forward-only** — there is no down-path. Redeploying an
134	earlier `vX.Y.Z` tag is safe **only** when the schema change was
135	backward-compatible. If it wasn't, roll back by restoring the database from the
136	Litestream replica to a point *before* the promote, rather than by redeploying
137	old code against a newer schema.
138	
139	:::note[Inspect without rolling back]
140	To look inside the replica without touching production, restore a throwaway copy
141	and query it with `sqlite3` — no rollback required. The repository's operator
142	debug kit documents this runbook.
143	:::
144	
145	:::caution[Verify your restore path before you need it]
146	A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Do a restore into a
147	throwaway copy at least once so you know the bucket, credentials, and endpoint are
148	right before an incident forces the question.
149	:::
150

1 --- 2 title: Console screens 3 description: A visual tour of the Custos operator console — claim codes, accounts, devices, moderation, the audit log, transfers, and server status. 4 --- 5 6 A tour of the Custos operator console (the admin companion app). Every image here is 7 generated automatically from the app's own browser test harness across named scenarios, 8 including a degraded relay, so the pictures track the real UI and cannot quietly drift. 9 10 :::note[These are browser renders, not device captures] 11 These screenshots come from running the app frontend in a browser (the test harness), 12 not from an iPhone. Layout, copy, and states are faithful, but device-only details are 13 **not** pictured: the biometric (Face ID / Touch ID) gate that precedes every signing 14 action, the Secure Enclave-held admin key, camera QR scanning on the Pair screen, the 15 system share sheet, and iOS safe-area insets and font rendering. Treat these as accurate 16 diagrams, not pixel-exact device photos. 17 ::: 18 19 ## Home — mint a claim code 20 21 The console opens on the active relay, ready to mint a single-use, device-signed account 22 claim code. A **Relay federation** block up top reports whether the upstream relay is 23 actually crawling this server — status, exact events behind, last seen — with a 24 **Request crawl** re-invite (see 25 [Is the upstream relay seeing you?](/operator/running-a-relay/#is-the-upstream-relay-seeing-you)). 26 27 31 32 Before any relay is paired, the console asks you to pair this operator device. 33 34 38 39 ## Pairing 40 41 Pair a device with a relay by QR or manual entry. 42 43 47 48 ## Accounts 49 50 Every account on one relay, searchable by handle or DID, with a per-row blob-quota 51 readout. 52 53 57 58 ## Claim codes 59 60 The claim-code inventory splits live credentials from terminal history. 61 62 66 67 ## Devices 68 69 Every admin device registered on one relay — active and revoked — with a remote revoke 70 for a lost device. 71 72 76 77 ## Moderation 78 79 Account takedown and restore, then credential revocation — each an armed, biometric-gated 80 destructive action. 81 82 86 87 ## Audit log 88 89 Every privileged operator action — takedowns, credential sweeps, code mints and 90 revokes, device pairings and revocations, transfer cancels, account repairs, 91 crawl requests — is durably recorded with the credential that signed it: the 92 master token or the specific paired device. The Audit screen browses the trail 93 reverse-chronologically, filterable by action, with per-event drill-in by actor 94 or subject. 95 96 100 101 ## Transfers 102 103 In-flight device transfers an operator can watch and cancel. 104 105 109 110 ## Server status 111 112 One relay's health as it reports it — version and uptime, account counts, blob and block 113 totals, firehose state, and background-sweep last-runs. Facts only; nothing here is a 114 verdict. 115 116 120 121 On a degraded relay, a troubled background sweep is flagged with a trailing `!` glyph and a 122 named fault — `stale` when its passes have stopped completing (the sweep is dead), or 123 `failed ` when a pass ran but recorded `n` errors (for blob GC, an account whose 124 reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs stay uncollected — and its disk unreclaimed — 125 until the fault is fixed). Naming each fault keeps the two 126 legible apart on a row that carries both; status is never signalled by colour alone. 127 128 132 133 ## Settings 134 135 Per-relay pairings, the global admin key, and the biometric toggle. 136 137 141 142 Further down, a **Diagnostics** section exports a redacted, per-relay network-error log for 143 troubleshooting — operation names, relay hosts, statuses, and short error codes only, never 144 credentials, keys, signed requests, or claim codes. 145 146 150

1	---
2	title: Configuration
3	description: The configuration and environment surface that tunes a deployment.
4	---
5	
6	A Custos deployment is configured through environment variables and a small set
7	of runtime settings. This page is the operator's map of that surface — the
8	knobs you'll actually set, with the context to set them safely. The exhaustive,
9	drift-proof inventory of every setting is the
10	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/), produced
11	directly from the server's configuration types.
12	
13	Some of these settings change what your server *advertises* to clients, not just
14	how it behaves: `describeServer` names the capabilities this deployment offers,
15	and clients enable features accordingly. See
16	[Capabilities](/operator/capabilities/) for which settings those are.
17	
18	## Secrets
19	
20	These are injected at runtime and never baked into the image:
21	
22	| Variable | Role |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` | Master key (64 hex chars = 32 bytes) — the AES-256-GCM key that encrypts all at-rest signing material: every account's repo signing key, the server's OAuth signing key, the JWT secret, and the node identity. |
25	| `EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN` | Bearer token guarding the admin/operator endpoints. |
26	
27	:::danger[The master key must never change out from under the database]
28	The master key **is** the AES-256-GCM key those secrets are encrypted with; it is
29	used directly. Changing the environment variable alone on a populated instance
30	makes all existing secrets undecryptable — the server fails to load account repo
31	signing keys, and repo writes break. **Losing it is unrecoverable.** So: store it
32	in a secret manager (agenix / sops / your platform's secret store) never in the
33	repository or the image, and back it up.
34	
35	If it's already lost or you suspect it's compromised, stop and follow the
36	[master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/) rather than
37	improvising — the recovery order matters.
38	:::
39	
40	Rotation is supported, but only as a deliberate offline operation: the
41	`pds rewrap-master-key` subcommand re-encrypts every stored secret from the old
42	key to the new one in a single atomic transaction, with the server stopped. Old
43	and new keys are supplied via `EZPDS_REWRAP_OLD_MASTER_KEY` /
44	`EZPDS_REWRAP_NEW_MASTER_KEY` environment variables (never CLI arguments), a
45	wrong old key aborts with no writes, and only after the re-wrap succeeds do you
46	point `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` at the new key and restart. Never rotate by
47	changing the environment variable alone.
48	
49	## Runtime
50	
51	| Variable | Role |
52	| --- | --- |
53	| `PORT` | Injected by the platform; the server binds it. |
54	| `EZPDS_PUBLIC_URL` | The externally reachable origin of the PDS. |
55	| `EZPDS_AVAILABLE_USER_DOMAINS` | Domains users may claim handles on. |
56	| `EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED` | Comma-separated labeler DIDs to watch; hosted accounts they label are flagged on the operator console. Off (empty) by default — see [Moderation § Labeler watching](/operator/moderation/#labeler-watching--flagged-accounts). |
57	
58	The table above is the operator-facing subset. Every remaining setting — with
59	its type, default, and doc-comment — is in the
60	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).

This surface reports the literal truth of what the machine is 8 doing — it does not hide the machinery. 9 10 If you are _using_ an identity rather than running a server, you want 11 [Using Obsign](/user/) instead. 12 13 17 18 ## What you run 19 20 - **[Running a relay](/operator/running-a-relay/)** — stand up the PDS, its 21 health, and what you are (and aren't) responsible for. 22 - **[Configuration](/operator/configuration/)** — the config and environment 23 surface that tunes a deployment. 24 - **[Moderation](/operator/moderation/)** — takedown, restore, credential 25 revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 26 - **[Master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)** — what to 27 do if the KEK is lost or compromised. 28 29 ## Which key you hold 30 31 The one thing to internalize before running Custos: you hold the **last** 32 rotation key, not the first. 33 34 ```text 35 rotationKeys[0] → the user's device key (highest precedence) 36 rotationKeys[1] → the user's recovery key (from their 2-of-3 backup) 37 rotationKeys[2] → the server's key (yours, lowest precedence) 38 ``` 39 40 Accounts created before on-device recovery keys carry two entries — the user's 41 device key, then yours — until their wallet adds the recovery key; your key is 42 last either way. The user can always override you. That is by design: it is what lets a user 43 leave your server without your permission, and it is the property that makes 44 hosting trustworthy rather than custodial. 45

a trailing `!` glyph and a named fault. A sweep whose last completed pass keeps
ageing reads `stale` — passes have stopped completing, so the sweep is dead. One
that completed but skipped work reads `failed <n>` — it ran, yet recorded `n`
errors (for blob GC, an account whose reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs
stay uncollected until the fault is fixed). The two are named so they read apart on a
row that has both, and _what_ degraded is legible without relying on color.

do not know the field ignore it.

skills.name: pr-review-comments
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

# Writing Clearly and Concisely

## Overview

William Strunk Jr.'s *The Elements of Style* (1918) teaches you to write clearly and cut ruthlessly.

**WARNING:** `elements-of-style.md` consumes ~12,000 tokens. Read it only when writing or editing prose.

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill whenever you write prose for humans:

- Documentation, README files, technical explanations
- Commit messages, pull request descriptions
- Error messages, UI copy, help text, comments
- Reports, summaries, or any explanation
- Editing to improve clarity

**If you're writing sentences for a human to read, use this skill.**

## Limited Context Strategy

When context is tight:
1. Write your draft using judgment
2. Dispatch a subagent with your draft and `elements-of-style.md`
3. Have the subagent copyedit and return the revision

## All Rules

### Elementary Rules of Usage (Grammar/Punctuation)
1. Form possessive singular by adding 's
2. Use comma after each term in series except last
3. Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
4. Comma before conjunction introducing co-ordinate clause
5. Don't join independent clauses by comma
6. Don't break sentences in two
7. Participial phrase at beginning refers to grammatical subject

### Elementary Principles of Composition
8. One paragraph per topic
9. Begin paragraph with topic sentence
10. **Use active voice**
11. **Put statements in positive form**
12. **Use definite, specific, concrete language**
13. **Omit needless words**
14. Avoid succession of loose sentences
15. Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form
16. **Keep related words together**
17. Keep to one tense in summaries
18. **Place emphatic words at end of sentence**

### Section V: Words and Expressions Commonly Misused
Alphabetical reference for usage questions

## Bottom Line

Writing for humans? Read `elements-of-style.md` and apply the rules. Low on tokens? Dispatch a subagent to copyedit with the guide.

# Writing for a Technical Audience

## Overview

**Core principle:** Technical writing must be clear, concise, and authentic. Clarity and technical depth are not opposites - you can have both. Avoid AI writing patterns that make content feel robotic or inauthentic.
￼
**Why this matters:** Developers value their time. Clear documentation builds trust. AI-like writing patterns (identified through research) make content feel generic and untrustworthy. Technical depth without clarity frustrates users. Clarity without depth leaves them stuck.

## When to Use

**Use this skill when:**
- Writing API documentation or references
- Creating guides, tutorials, or how-to content
- Documenting code, features, or architecture
- Writing technical blog posts or articles
- Reviewing technical content for clarity

**Trigger symptoms:**
- "Does this sound too robotic?"
- Writing feels formal or stiff
- Using phrases like "delve into" or "leverage"
- Explaining obvious things instead of getting to the point
- Uncertain if content is clear enough

## The Three Pillars

### 1. Clarity

Developers should understand on first read. No re-reading required.

**Techniques:**
- Short sentences (15-20 words average)
- Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences)
- Active voice over passive
- One concept per paragraph
- Define technical terms on first use

### 2. Conciseness

Every word serves a purpose. Remove noise and filler.

**Techniques:**
- Delete throat-clearing ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- Cut hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- Remove marketing fluff ("powerful," "robust," "seamless")
- Use direct language ("use" not "leverage," "show" not "illuminate")

### 3. Consistency

Same terminology, structure, and voice throughout.

**Techniques:**
- Pick one term and stick to it (not "endpoint," "URL," "route" interchangeably)
- Use consistent code formatting
- Maintain same tone across all content
- Follow established patterns for similar content types

## Avoid AI Writing Patterns

Research shows specific phrases and structures that readers identify as AI-generated. Avoid these to maintain authenticity.

### AI Phrases to Never Use

| AI Phrase | Why It's Bad | Use Instead |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| "delve into" | Overly formal, 269x spike post-ChatGPT | "explore," "examine," "look at" |
| "leverage" | Corporate jargon | "use," "take advantage of" |
| "robust" / "seamless" | Vague marketing adjectives | Be specific about what you mean |
| "at its core" | Condescending simplification | "fundamentally" (use rarely) or delete |
| "cutting-edge" / "revolutionary" | Empty hype | Describe actual features |
| "streamline" / "optimize" | Vague promises | "speed up," "reduce," "improve" |
| "foster" / "cultivate" | Bland corporate speak | Use direct action verbs |
| "unlock the potential" | Cliched metaphor | State specific outcome |
| "in today's fast-paced world" | Generic filler | Delete entirely |
| "needless to say" | If needless, don't say it | Delete |

### Throat-Clearing to Delete

**Never start with:**
- "Let me explain..."
- "It's important to note that..."
- "It's worth noting..."
- "In essence..."
- "Let's explore..."

**Fix:** Start with substance. Delete the preamble.

### Hedging Language to Eliminate

| Hedged | Confident |
|--------|-----------|
| "I think we should..." | "We should..." |
| "It would be great if..." | "Please do X" |
| "Should be able to..." | "Can complete..." |
| "Basically..." | Delete it |
| "Generally speaking..." | Be specific or remove |
| "One might argue..." | "This indicates..." |

**Why hedging fails:** Makes you sound uncertain even when you're correct. State facts directly.

### Transition Word Overuse

AI defaults to formal Victorian-era connectors. Use simpler alternatives or break paragraphs.

| Overused AI | Better |
|------------|--------|
| Moreover / Furthermore | Plus, also, and |
| However / Nevertheless | But, though, still |
| Additionally | And, plus |
| Consequently / As a result | So, then |
| That being said | But (or delete) |
| Indeed / Interestingly | Often delete entirely |
| In conclusion | End cleanly without announcing it |

## Technical Writing Patterns

### Explain WHY for These Cases

**ALWAYS explain why when:**

1. **Design decisions with tradeoffs**
   - Good: "We use pagination instead of cursors because it's simpler for most use cases and maintains consistent ordering"
   - Bad: "We use pagination" (no context for when to deviate)

2. **Non-obvious patterns**
   - Good: "Row Level Security must be enabled on all tables exposed via the Data API because it enforces security at the database level, preventing bypass through direct SQL access"
   - Bad: "Enable RLS on all tables" (why?)

3. **Breaking from conventions**
   - Good: "This API uses POST for reads because GET requests can't include request bodies in some HTTP clients"
   - Bad: "Use POST to fetch data" (violates REST conventions without justification)

**When "how" alone suffices:**
- Mechanical steps with no alternatives ("Click Save")
- Standard practices ("Use npm install")
- When you genuinely don't know why (document behavior, note uncertainty)

### Code Examples: One Excellent Example

**Don't:**
- Implement in 5 languages
- Create fill-in-the-blank templates
- Write perfect-world examples with no error handling

**Do:**
- One complete, runnable example
- Include error handling
- Show realistic usage
- Comment WHY, not what

**Good Example Pattern:**

```python
# Good: Complete, realistic, explains why
try:
    response = await fetch_user(user_id)
    # Check status before assuming success - API returns 200 for "not found"
    if response.status != 200:
        raise APIError(f"Failed to fetch user: {response.status}")
    return response.json()
except NetworkError as e:
    # Network failures are retryable - log and re-raise for retry logic
    logger.warning(f"Network error fetching user {user_id}: {e}")
    raise
```

**Bad Example Pattern:**

```python
# Bad: Perfect world, no context, brittle
response = await fetch_user(user_id)
return response.json()
```

### Progressive Disclosure

Layer complexity. Simple first, then depth.

**Pattern:**
1. **Basic explanation** - what it does, core concept
2. **Simple example** - minimal working code
3. **Advanced section** - edge cases, configuration, tradeoffs
4. **Reference** - complete API surface

**Good:**
```markdown
## Authentication

All API requests require an API key in the Authorization header:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer REDACTED" https://api.example.com/users
```

### Advanced: Token Rotation

For production systems, rotate API keys every 90 days...
```

**Bad:**
```markdown
## Authentication

Authentication can be performed using several methods including API keys, OAuth 2.0, or JWT tokens. The choice depends on your security requirements, user experience goals, and architectural constraints. Let's explore each option...
```

(Too much upfront. Start simple.)

## Anti-Patterns from Real Documentation

### 1. Assumes Too Much

**Bad:**
> "Simply connect your ETLOrchestrator to the HydraNode endpoint. Once a connection is established, instantiate a DataStream by passing your KinesisConfiguration."

**Why it fails:** Jargon firehose with no definitions, no links, no onramp for beginners.

**Fix:** Define terms, link to prerequisites, provide Getting Started guide.

### 2. Perfect World Examples

**Bad:**
```javascript
const myFile = document.getElementById('file-input').files[0];
const response = await uploadFile('/api/upload', myFile);
console.log('File uploaded successfully!');
```

**Why it fails:** No error handling, ignores edge cases (no file selected, network failure, file too large).

**Fix:** Wrap in try-catch, check response status, handle undefined files.

### 3. Vague and Unhelpful

**Bad:**
- `getUser(userId)`: "Gets a user by their ID."
- `class DataProcessor`: "A class for processing data."
- `processData(data)`: "Processes the data."

**Why it fails:** Tautological. Says nothing beyond the function name.

**Fix:** Describe behavior, parameters, return values, exceptions. "Fetches user record from database, returns null if user doesn't exist. Throws AuthError if API key lacks read permissions."

## Pro-Examples from Industry Leaders

### Supabase (Clarity + Depth)

> "Row Level Security (RLS) is a PostgreSQL feature that allows you to control which rows a user can access in a table. When you enable RLS on a table, all SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations are subject to a security policy. A policy is a SQL expression that returns a boolean value. If the expression returns true, the operation is allowed to proceed. If it returns false or null, the operation is denied."

**Why it works:** Defines RLS, explains scope (CRUD operations), defines mechanism (policy = SQL boolean expression). Dense with information, perfectly clear.

### Stripe (Predictable Contract)

> "Stripe uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. In general: Codes in the 2xx range indicate success. Codes in the 4xx range indicate an error that failed given the information provided. Codes in the 5xx range indicate an error with Stripe's servers."

**Why it works:** Establishes predictable contract for fundamental API behavior. Technical, precise, immediately useful.

### Astro (Anticipates Questions)

> "You can run create-astro anywhere on your machine, so you don't have to create an empty directory for your project first. If you don't have an empty directory yet, the wizard will help you create one."

**Why it works:** Anticipates common beginner question ("Do I need to make a folder first?") and answers it proactively.

### Tailwind CSS (Teaches Philosophy)

> "The biggest maintainability concern when using a utility-first approach is managing commonly repeated utility combinations. The traditional approach is to extract repeated utilities into a component class. We believe that @apply should be used sparingly. The best way to manage repeated utility combinations is to create reusable components with a templating language."

**Why it works:** Identifies problem, presents common solution, explains why that solution is suboptimal, guides toward better approach. Teaches philosophy, not just features.

## Writing That Feels Human

### Use Contractions

**AI defaults to:**
- "It is important that you do not..."
- "You will need to..."

**Human writing:**
- "It's important that you don't..."
- "You'll need to..."

### Vary Sentence Length

**AI writes:**
Every paragraph is 3-4 sentences. Every sentence is 15-20 words. Everything feels perfectly balanced and rhythmic in an uncanny way.

**Human writes:**
Short sentences create emphasis. Longer sentences provide context, explanation, or explore nuance that requires more breathing room. Mix them. Create rhythm naturally.

### Add Personality

**AI avoids:**
- First person ("I," "we")
- Opinions
- Personal anecdotes
- Humor

**Human includes:**
- "We tried the obvious solution first and it failed"
- "I found this approach more practical because..."
- Opinions grounded in experience
- Self-aware observations

### Break Grammar Rules Intentionally

**AI never:**
- Starts sentences with "And" or "But"
- Uses sentence fragments
- Ends with prepositions

**Human does:**
- "And that's exactly the point." (emphasis)
- "This is what we're dealing with." (natural)

### Be Specific

**AI writes vaguely:**
- "This approach offers significant benefits"
- "Companies have seen improved results"

**Human writes specifically:**
- "We reduced latency from 450ms to 120ms"
- "Three team members raised concerns about X"

## Code Comments and Documentation

### Punctuation

Always use periods at the end of code comments.

```typescript
// Good: Validates user input before processing.
// Bad: validates user input before processing
```

### Headings

Use sentence case in all headings. Never title case.

```markdown
Good: ## Error handling patterns
Bad:  ## Error Handling Patterns

Good: ### When to use async
Bad:  ### When To Use Async
```

### Error Messages

Format error messages as lowercase sentence fragments. They compose naturally when chained.

```
Good: failed to parse configuration: invalid JSON at line 42
Bad:  Failed to Parse Configuration: Invalid JSON at Line 42
```

The lowercase format works because errors often chain: `"operation failed: " + innerError.message` reads correctly.

## Red Flags - Review Checklist

Before publishing, check for these issues:

- [ ] No AI phrases ("delve," "leverage," "robust," "at its core")
- [ ] No throat-clearing openings ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- [ ] No hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- [ ] No marketing fluff ("powerful," "revolutionary," "cutting-edge")
- [ ] Sentence length varies (not all 15-20 words)
- [ ] Paragraph length varies (not all 3-4 sentences)
- [ ] Contractions used naturally ("it's" not "it is")
- [ ] Active voice, clear actors (not "it can be seen that")
- [ ] Code examples include error handling
- [ ] WHY explained for design decisions
- [ ] Technical terms defined on first use
- [ ] Specific numbers/names/details (not vague claims)
- [ ] Read aloud test - does it sound natural?
- [ ] Code comments end with periods
- [ ] Headings use sentence case (not Title Case)
- [ ] Error messages are lowercase sentence fragments

## Common Mistakes and Fixes

| Mistake | Reality | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| "Just being thorough with explanations" | You're explaining obvious things. | Delete explanations of what developers already know. |
| "Keeping it professional with formal language" | Formal = robotic. | Use contractions, conversational tone, natural language. |
| "Covering all the edge cases upfront" | Overwhelms reader. | Basic case first, advanced section for edge cases. |
| "Using precise technical terminology" | Jargon without definitions loses readers. | Define terms on first use, link to glossary. |
| "Being careful with hedging language" | Hedging makes you sound uncertain. | State facts directly. Remove qualifiers. |
| "Perfect code examples look cleaner" | Perfect world examples are brittle in practice. | Include error handling, show realistic usage. |
| "More examples = more helpful" | Too many examples = noise. | One excellent, complete example beats five shallow ones. |

## Summary

**Technical writing in three rules:**

1. **Clear and concise** - Short sentences, short paragraphs, active voice, no filler
2. **Authentic voice** - Contractions, varied rhythm, personality, specific details
3. **Explain why** - Design decisions, tradeoffs, non-obvious patterns need justification

**Avoid AI markers:** No "delve," "leverage," "robust." No throat-clearing. No hedging. No formal transitions.

**One excellent example** beats five mediocre ones. Include error handling. Show realistic usage.

**Technical depth + clarity are not opposites.** You can have both. Supabase, Stripe, and Cloudflare prove this daily.

**Read aloud test:** If it sounds robotic or overly formal, rewrite it.

1	# Writing style guide
2	
3	Last verified: 2026-08-02
4	
5	Rules for every prose surface in this repo: the docs site, marketing copy, in-app
6	strings, code comments, and AGENTS.md files. The dream routine and doc-editing
7	agents follow this file; human PRs are reviewed against it.
8	
9	## Audiences
10	
11	**Obsign (user tier: `sites/docs` `user/`, in-app copy, marketing).**
12	Write for the *release* audience: security-minded people in the 1Password /
13	Proton lane, including people who are not technical but want better security
14	hygiene. The early test audience (peers, protocol-adjacent Bluesky users) can
15	read down to this register; the release audience cannot read up to a
16	protocol-native one. Concretely:
17	
18	- Lead with what can go wrong and how Obsign protects against it. Data
19	  ownership and sovereignty are outcomes the reader discovers, not the pitch —
20	  there is credible skepticism, even among protocol-minded users, that "owning
21	  your data" sells on its own.
22	- Protocol machinery (DID methods, rotation keys, PLC) appears only behind
23	  clearly-marked Advanced sections or on reference pages. A first-run page never
24	  requires it. The in-app register ("What's your situation?") is the model.
25	
26	**Custos (operator tier: `sites/docs` `operator/`, deploy/ops docs).**
27	A technical-minded subset of Obsign users who care how the technology works and
28	want full control over their data and presence. Keep the depth; these readers
29	want mechanism. The voice rules below still apply — technical is not the same
30	as dense.
31	
32	## Voice
33	
34	The failure mode to avoid is uniform, machine-flavored prose. The tells, and
35	their fixes:
36	
37	- **Em-dash budget.** A handful per page, not one per sentence. Most asides
38	  read fine as a separate sentence or set off with commas.
39	- **Retire the contrast scaffold.** "X is not Y — it's Z" and "not X, but Y"
40	  are fine once; as the default sentence shape they are a fingerprint. Say what
41	  a thing *is*.
42	- **No self-defense.** Cut asides that argue the design is right ("which is
43	  exactly the right time", "the trade is real"). Users need the task done, not
44	  the decision justified. Rationale belongs in ADRs.
45	- **Drop defensive adverbs.** "deliberately", "exactly", "precisely",
46	  "load-bearing" are for design docs. In user prose they signal an author
47	  anticipating an argument no reader is making.
48	- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences exist. Use them.
49	- **Contractions are fine.** "It's" and "don't" read as human; "it is" and
50	  "do not" at every occurrence read as generated.
51	- Standard hygiene: active voice, concrete specifics over vague claims, no
52	  throat-clearing openers, no marketing adjectives ("robust", "seamless").
53	
54	The read-aloud test catches most violations: if a paragraph sounds like a
55	narrator defending a thesis, rewrite it as a person explaining a task.
56	
57	## Where prose lives
58	
59	One fact, one home. The repo's parity-check scripts exist because duplicated
60	prose drifts; the cheaper fix is not duplicating it.
61	
62	- **Code comments state constraints the code can't show** — invariants,
63	  ordering requirements, why an obvious alternative is wrong. They do not
64	  narrate what the next line does, and they do not argue rationale at length:
65	  link the ADR instead.
66	- **Don't restate what a test enforces.** If a test pins the behavior, the
67	  comment states the invariant in a line or two and names the test.
68	- **AGENTS.md is a map, not the territory.** An entry is a few lines: what the
69	  module is, the one or two facts an agent needs before opening it, and a
70	  pointer to the module doc. The detailed prose lives in exactly one place,
71	  nearest the code — usually the module doc. When consolidating, move detail
72	  *toward* the code and leave AGENTS.md pointing at it, never the reverse.
73	- **ADRs and design plans own rationale.** A comment or doc that finds itself
74	  explaining *why the design is right* should shrink to a link.
75	
76	## Enforcement
77	
78	By review, not by gate. Style is judgment work; the dream routine applies this
79	file on its nightly pass, and reviewers hold PRs to it. If a rule here proves
80	wrong in practice, change the rule — this file is the spec, not a monument.

# Writing style guide

Last verified: 2026-08-02

Rules for every prose surface in this repo: the docs site, marketing copy, in-app
strings, code comments, and AGENTS.md files. The dream routine and doc-editing
agents follow this file; human PRs are reviewed against it.

## Audiences

**Obsign (user tier: `sites/docs` `user/`, in-app copy, marketing).**
Write for the *release* audience: security-minded people in the 1Password /
Proton lane, including people who are not technical but want better security
hygiene. The early test audience (peers, protocol-adjacent Bluesky users) can
read down to this register; the release audience cannot read up to a
protocol-native one. Concretely:

- Lead with what can go wrong and how Obsign protects against it. Data
  ownership and sovereignty are outcomes the reader discovers, not the pitch —
  there is credible skepticism, even among protocol-minded users, that "owning
  your data" sells on its own.
- Protocol machinery (DID methods, rotation keys, PLC) appears only behind
  clearly-marked Advanced sections or on reference pages. A first-run page never
  requires it. The in-app register ("What's your situation?") is the model.

**Custos (operator tier: `sites/docs` `operator/`, deploy/ops docs).**
A technical-minded subset of Obsign users who care how the technology works and
want full control over their data and presence. Keep the depth; these readers
want mechanism. The voice rules below still apply — technical is not the same
as dense.

## Voice

The failure mode to avoid is uniform, machine-flavored prose. The tells, and
their fixes:

- **Em-dash budget.** A handful per page, not one per sentence. Most asides
  read fine as a separate sentence or set off with commas.
- **Retire the contrast scaffold.** "X is not Y — it's Z" and "not X, but Y"
  are fine once; as the default sentence shape they are a fingerprint. Say what
  a thing *is*.
- **No self-defense.** Cut asides that argue the design is right ("which is
  exactly the right time", "the trade is real"). Users need the task done, not
  the decision justified. Rationale belongs in ADRs.
- **Drop defensive adverbs.** "deliberately", "exactly", "precisely",
  "load-bearing" are for design docs. In user prose they signal an author
  anticipating an argument no reader is making.
- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences exist. Use them.
- **Contractions are fine.** "It's" and "don't" read as human; "it is" and
  "do not" at every occurrence read as generated.
- Standard hygiene: active voice, concrete specifics over vague claims, no
  throat-clearing openers, no marketing adjectives ("robust", "seamless").

The read-aloud test catches most violations: if a paragraph sounds like a
narrator defending a thesis, rewrite it as a person explaining a task.

## Where prose lives

One fact, one home. The repo's parity-check scripts exist because duplicated
prose drifts; the cheaper fix is not duplicating it.

- **Code comments state constraints the code can't show** — invariants,
  ordering requirements, why an obvious alternative is wrong. They do not
  narrate what the next line does, and they do not argue rationale at length:
  link the ADR instead.

  explaining *why the design is right* should shrink to a link.

## Enforcement

By review, not by gate. Style is judgment work; the dream routine applies this
file on its nightly pass, and reviewers hold PRs to it. If a rule here proves
wrong in practice, change the rule — this file is the spec, not a monument.

Obsign
Obsign Custos GitHub

Privacy

This site runs cookieless, self-hosted analytics. No third party ever sees your visit, and nothing you read here follows you anywhere else.

We run our own instance of Umami, an open-source analytics tool, to see which pages get read and where visitors come from. It sets no cookies and stores no cross-site identifier: there is nothing here to opt out of because there is nothing that tracks you between sites or across visits.

What it records per page view: the page, the referrer, and coarse browser/OS/device and country information. Your IP address is never stored — Umami hashes it together with your browser and this site's ID, using a salt it rotates every day, purely to distinguish a return visit from a new one within that day. The raw address never touches disk.

This applies to Obsign and Custos, the two pages of this marketing site — and nowhere else. It is never present in the Obsign or Admin Companion apps, on the Custos server itself, or on any page that touches your account, your identity, or your keys.

The dashboard lives on infrastructure we operate; the data never leaves it, and it is never sold or shared. The source for this site is public, same as everything else we run.

The TestFlight waitlist is the one place this site asks for anything: an email address, and optionally an AT Protocol handle. Both go straight to our own server (Custos) and nowhere else. The email is used once — to send your TestFlight invite — and never shared; the handle is read only as a “coming with an existing account” signal, and we never touch the account itself. Analytics sees none of it: the signup event records only that a signup happened, never the address or handle.

Obsign — the identity wallet Custos — the personal data server
Open source (ezpds) · built on the AT Protocol
